speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: STATEMENT REGARDING EXCHANGE OF INFORMATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, is the Minister of Trade and Commerce in a position today to give the
house any further information with respect to the question I asked him on Friday which had to do with whether Canada is to get all the atomic information that is being exchanged between the United States and Great Britain?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: STATEMENT REGARDING EXCHANGE OF INFORMATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the information requested. An announcement was made last Friday of amendments to the United States-United Kingdom bilateral agreement to provide for the following:
(a)	An exchange of information on the development, design, construction, operation and use of certain package power reactors and reactors for the propulsion of naval vessels, aircraft and land vehicles; and
(b)	The transfer as between the United States and the United Kingdom of certain fissionable materials. Specifically, the amendment will permit the United Kingdom atomic energy authority to purchase U-235 from the United States atomic energy commission. It will also permit the United Kingdom atomic energy authority to sell to the United States atomic energy commission certain quantities of depleted uranium.
The United States atomic energy commission has proposed that our bilateral be amended as per (a) above. It should be noted that in our existing bilateral there is a provision covering the exchange of information on package reactors. The amendment will provide for the inclusion of information on submarine, ship and aircraft reactors.
With respect to (b) above, our existing bilateral does provide for the transfer of fissionable materials as between the two countries. We are now selling natural uranium, plutonium and depleted uranium to the United States atomic energy commission and we have the right to purchase U-235 up to an enrichment of 20 per cent. In other words, the present United States-Canada bilateral does not require amendment in so far as it affects the transfer of fissionable materials as between the two countries.

should like to ask a question of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. On May 28 last, in reply to a question by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that in 1951, 195,000 cases of eggs were exported from Canada and 95,000

speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: ALLEGED IMPORTS FROM IRON CURTAIN COUNTRIES
speechtext: -that these 95,000 cases of eggs, or any part of them, were imported from behind the iron curtain?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: ALLEGED IMPORTS FROM IRON CURTAIN COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon, member was good enough to give me notice of his question and I have been able to look up the statistics. I find that the statement referred to is completely false. There were no importations of eggs to Canada from countries behind the iron curtain in 1951. The 95,000 cases of eggs were imported from the following countries: United States of America, Holland and Eire. The reason for importation in 1951 was the short supply of eggs in Canada at that time.
The average price of eggs to producers in Canada in 1951 was the highest average price in Canada for the years 1950-1955 inclusive.
The recent shipment of 10,000 cases of eggs from Poland was the first shipment into Canada from Poland. Egg prices have gone up in Canada since that shipment was received.

speakeroldname: Hon. Roberl H. Winters (Minister of Public Works) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING APPROVAL BY MINISTER, ETC.
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 388, to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act.
He said: This bill seeks to amend part I of the Navigable Waters Protection Act, which is that part of the statute administered by the Department of Public Works.
This part of the act, as it presently stands, provides that no work shall be built in a navigable water unless the governor in council has first approved of the plan and site of the work. Persons proposing to construct works in navigable waters are required to submit a plan of the work and a description of the site to the Minister of Public Works. Public notice of the proposal is also required. To this end applicants must deposit a copy of the plan and description in the local land registry office and insert an advertisement in the Canada Gazette as well as in two local newspapers. One month must elapse after the advertising is thus inserted before the application can be submitted to the governor in council.
Our navigable waters have played a vital part in Canada's development and they continue to do so even though others forms of communication have rapidly developed over the years. One of nature's greatest gifts to Canada is a plentiful supply of rivers and lakes. The pioneer era of Canada was dominated by our rivers. The country was explored and opened up along their channels because they then were the only routes through a land of impenetrable forests. Exploration, settlement, trade and national development all have made use of them. At the time of confederation, by far the greatest part of what is now Canada was still dependent upon them.

Navigable Waters Protection Act
It is not too much to say, in fact, that in the first half of the 19th century Canada was dependent upon her waterways. In the second half, railways provided a new impetus and we have gone on from there to build up a transportation system which relies not on any one but on a number of methods of communication. I think hon. members will agree, however, that our navigable waters continue to be a crucial part of our entire transportation picture and nothing could more graphically illustrate this than that immense project which is now under way, namely, the St. Lawrence seaway.
This act we are seeking now to amend has been interwoven with a great deal of our economic history because it is the instrument the government has used for generations to protect the public interest in seeing that our navigable streams are protected for the use of navigation.
In the year 1886, the then minister of marine and fisheries, Hon. George Foster, moved for leave to introduce a bill respecting the protection of navigable waters, a piece of legislation which he said was mainly an adaptation of the law as it then existed, with some changes in the verbiage and two or three sections added. In other words, in one form or another, this law goes a long way back. The economic pulse of young Canada of 1886 can be sensed in reading the speeches made at that time because they largely revolve around the question of disposal in navigable streams of the immense quantities of sawdust arising from the great industry of the era, lumbering.
One can also catch in that debate of 1886 the voices of the rivalries between shipping interests and the lumbering firms whose enormous quantities of logs sometimes tended to choke our rivers from bank to bank.
A reading of that debate of 1886 leaves no doubt that our parliamentary predecessors felt it important that our navigable waters should be protected and that every reasonable precaution should be taken before authority was granted to permit structures to be built in them. I think it is agreed that this need is as important today as it was then.
However, it has been found that the procedures required by the present statute involve long delays in obtaining the approval of the governor in council. These delays are particularly onerous in these days of rapid development; and the statute is specific in requiring that the approval of the governor in council be obtained before construction of the work is commenced. Moreover, if a structure is started without the necessary approval there is no authority whatever under the statute for giving it subsequent approval.

Even having regard to the essential character of our navigable waters and the importance of protecting them, the present statute seems too rigid for present-day application. The number of applications received is quite high and it is on the increase. Last year, for example, approximately 300 applications were processed. It is desirable, therefore, that procedures be developed which will allow applications to be processed expeditiously. This bill seeks to simplify the procedures without sacrificing the element of protection. It provides that the Minister of Public Works may approve the plan and site, thereby reducing the delays involved in referring to the governor in council the multitude of applications, many of them minor in importance and involving only small amounts of money. Further provision is made to enable the Minister of Public Works to approve the plan and site after construction has been commenced if, before commencing construction, the applicant has obtained in writing the consent of the Minister of Public Works.
Under the statute as it now stands, there are certain exemptions, namely, small wharves, groynes, bank and beach protection works or boathouses that do not interfere with navigation and do not cost more than $1,000. These the minister is authorized to approve without the application having to pass through all the stages required by the statute for larger projects.
This bill enlarges this scope and makes exemptions applicable to all works other than certain specific types which, no matter how inexpensive, will interfere with navigation. The works which will not be exempted are bridges, dams, booms, aboiteaux or causeways. The limitation of $1,000 which was enacted many years ago is now considered unrealistic and the bill raises this to $5,000.
At present a lawful work may be rebuilt or repaired if in the opinion of the minister such rebuilding or repairing does not increase the interference with navigation. Many persons desire to change a work in such a way that it will not increase substantially the interference with navigation, but because the change cannot be called rebuilding or repairing they are required to conform to all the formal steps required by the statute. The bill simplifies this procedure in the case of any alteration which would not substantially increase the interference with navigation.
The statute now provides that if a work was built or was in the process of construction on the first day of June, 1938, without the approval of the governor in council subsequent approval may be sought.

Nothing built since that time can be approved unless the provisions of the statute have been fully complied with.
Since June 1, 1938 some works have been constructed without approval. As I have indicated, as the statute now stands, they are not capable of being approved. It is considered that if an unapproved work merits approval and has been in existence for a reasonable period of time without creating navigational difficulties there should be authority to approve it. The bill establishes this period as five years.
It is considered that the changes will simplify the act and facilitate its administration without reducing the protection which the government considers should be exercised over our navigable waters.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING APPROVAL BY MINISTER, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister in opening the debate on this bill dealt at some length with the importance of the Navigable Waters Protection Act and if I heard him correctly he used words to this effect, that navigable waters should continue to be a crucial part of our transportation system. That, of course, is very true but I am afraid at least some of the terms of this bill are removing the restrictions to a greater extent than is necessary to meet modern conditions. After all, once a work of this kind is placed in a navigable water it is there for many, many years and it is very difficult to do anything about it. If navigation happens to be impeded by that work then there is no way of meeting that situation, that is in ordinary practice, and the particular lake, river, bay or harbour is impeded to the extent that work has been erected.
The act, of course, was designed as a means of helping transport by water, of insuring that there would not be unreasonable interference with that type of transportation. As the minister has said, the act has always been considered one of the most important acts on the statute books of Canada. It deals with a subject that is primarily the responsibility of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) and not the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) at all. I suggest the Minister of Public Works is in this picture only as a supernumerary. If one refers to the report of the Department of Transport he will find that part 2 of the Navigable Waters Protection Act is administered by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler), whereas part 1, which is the general overriding provision, has up to this time been the responsibility of the cabinet as a whole; as the minister will admit, the governor in council has been responsible for the proper carrying out of the first part of the Navigable Waters Protection Act.
Navigable Waters Protection Act
My first objection to this bill is that, should it become law, the cabinet will go right out of the picture and one minister aione, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters), will become the dictator, shall I say, under the Navigable Waters Protection Act. He is not responsible at all for water transport, which is the responsibility of the Minister of Transport, and yet the Minister of Public Works is to be given complete jurisdiction over obstructions placed in navigable waters.
I am concerned primarily with the position of the Minister of Transport, who is responsible for our national harbours, and also for seven harbour commissions which I believe have been incorporated under dominion statutes. There is a provision written into this bill which provides that the Minister of Transport must be consulted in certain cases, but he is not given the same power as that to be given to the Minister of Public Works even with regard to works erected in one of our great national harbours.
The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) has jurisdiction under the act passed last year over international rivers. If there were to be a work erected, say, on the Columbia or on the Saint John river, then the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources would have to issue a permit. Where is he to be in this picture? Under this bill the Minister of Public Works could authorize the erection of a dam, a pier or other obstruction on the Columbia, the Saint John or the Yukon river and the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources would have no authority whatever to interfere.
The Department of Fisheries should be concerned with obstructions placed in navigable waters, and it might be vital to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney) as to whether an obstruction should be permitted in waters where naval vessels are plying. There are many reasons why the decision as to what works should be erected in navigable waters should be placed before the cabinet as a whole rather than being left in the office of the Department of Public Works.
The Minister of Public Works, for whom I have great respect, is the minister from Nova Scotia, but under this bill he would be permitted to authorize works anywhere on the British Columbia coast and the ministers from British Columbia need not know anything about them. They would have no opportunity to deal with the application for a work of that kind. On the other hand, under the present act they would at least

Navigable Waters Protection Act have the opportunity to know because the application would have to be passed by the cabinet as a whole.
I suggest to the minister with great earnestness that it is much wiser to keep the decision in the hands of the cabinet with regard certainly to the major works that are going to be erected in navigable waters rather than to leave it to an individual minister. See what it places in the hands of one minister. The time may come when a minister of public works will be able to use this power for patronage purposes or for favouritism to this group or that group or this company or the other company. It is placing the minister's own department in an invidious position. Power of that type should not be given to one minister.
I am afraid this is just a case of the departmental officials thinking that they could get along a lot faster and with far less trouble if they did not have to present these applications to the cabinet, if they could just decide themselves that such and such a work would go in such and such a spot and then give the minister a memorandum and have approval of the scheme without all the fuss and bother of going to the cabinet. We have a cabinet in Canada which is for the very purpose of dealing with situations of this kind, of being there so that you get the judgment of the whole group, men who come from all parts of the country, rather than leaving decisions of this kind in the hands of one minister.
Under the act now in effect the key section is section 4. The first subsection of that section reads as follows:
No work shall be built or placed in, upon, over, under, through or across any navigable water unless the site thereof has been approved by the governor in council, nor unless such work is built, placed and maintained in accordance with plans and regulations approved or made by the governor in council.
That is the key section of the first part of the present act. In the next section, section 5, we find that any unauthorized works can only be removed by the authority of the governor in council. It is true that the cabinet can tell the Minister of Public Works to have that done but the authority rests with the governor in council. Furthermore, under the present law any regulations under the act have to be passed by the governor in council. Yet in the new bill the whole power to make regulations is taken away from the governor in council and placed in the hands of the Minister of Public Works alone. That, I suggest, is going too far and, frankly, I am hoping that the minister and the other members of the cabinet will be willing to have

a further look at the bill rather than try to force it through in the form in which it is presented to the house today.
Then, under the bill we are discussing there is this further power. The Minister of Public Works will be able simply to give a letter saying to a firm: You can go ahead and build that work. He can give that letter without even seeing a plan of the work in question. It is true that eventually the work will have to get approval and plans will have to be filed, but surely it is going too far to allow the minister simply to write a letter to the firm and that is all they require to construct the work. No work in Canada that is going to interfere with navigable waters is of that urgency.
For one thing, the people who are affected should be given time to file complaints. Suppose a logging company comes to the minister and gets a letter permitting it to put a boom at a certain spot which interferes with property abutting on the water. The owner of the land should have the right to make a complaint before consent is given to the placing of the boom. Yet under the bill as presented to the house the minister can authorize such a boom to be placed in those waters and there is no requirement whatever that anybody shall be given notice.
Perhaps with a boom it would be simpler. Possibly I have used a poor illustration because a boom can be moved. But suppose a pier or a dam or something of a permanent nature is installed. Then the owner of the abutting property is very seriously prejudiced. I suggest that the provisions in the original law calling for the filing of plans, advertising and giving people affected time to appear were very sound. They were put there for a very good reason and they should not be overridden at this time simply in order to get faster action in installing a pier or other work.
Furthermore, the minister spoke very favourably of the provision whereby if a work has been in place for five years it can then be authorized. Surely that undermines the whole working of the act. People should not be putting bridges, dams or obstructions of any kind in navigable waters without getting permission first. Yet here we are writing in a section which says to Mr. A or John Jones and Company Limited:	If you
put in a dam five years ago and have been able to get away with it, that is all right now and we will give you approval. I think that provision should be changed. I do not see any fairness in writing a provision of that type into the law.

The present act also includes a very wide definition of work as found in section 2 (b) which reads as follows:
"Work" includes any bridge, boom, dam, aboiteau, wharf, dock, pier or other structure, tunnel or pipe-
Of course, the word "pipe" is important now that pipe lines are being put under navigable waters.
[DOT]-or telegraph or power cable or wire and the approaches or other works necessary or appurtenant thereto, or any work, structure or device, whether similar in character to the foregoing or not. which may interfere with navigation.
That definition is very wide. It covers everything. But there is a provision written into the law at the present time for taking out certain specific works if they are of a value of $1,000 or less. That is contained in subsection 2 of section 4 which reads as follows:
The provisions of this section do not apply to small wharves or groynes or other bank or beach protection works, or boathouses, if in the opinion of the Minister of Public Works-
Here he was given discretion in the original act, and I think properly so.
-	(a) they do not interfere with navigation, and
-	(b) do not cost more than one thousand dollars.
That meant that the minister could exempt these small wharves or groynes or bank or beach protection works or boathouses from the act if they did not interfere with navigation and if they did not cost more than $1,000. But now in the new bill the minister goes at it the other way. He says that a bridge, boom, dam, aboiteau or causeway are in the first class and everything else, all these other things, wharves, docks, piers, tunnels, pipes, telegraph or power cables or wires and so on are in another class. They are all put in the category: "if, in his opinion, he thinks they do not substantially interfere with navigation"-the word "substantially" appears for the first time in this bill; it was not in the original act at all-and then in addition, "if the value of the work does not exceed $5,000" instead of $1,000. In other words, the minister will be able to exempt every work up to $5,000 in value if he thinks it does not substantially interfere wtih navigation, except in the case of a bridge, boom, dam, aboiteau or causeway. I think that is going rather far. I think it would be far better perhaps to extend the exemptions as contained in the present act rather than taking everything out except bridge, boom, dam, aboiteau and causeway.
I should like to comment on the effect of this bill on the harbours of Canada. I refer particularly to the national harbours and to those harbours which have harbour commissions. Of course, both types of harbours
18, 1956
Navigable Waters Protection Act come under the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler). The latter harbours are Belleville, Hamilton, New Westminster, north Fraser, Port Alberni, Toronto, Winnipeg and St. Boniface. Under this bill, as it stands, the Minister of Public Works can authorize any work in any one of those harbours that have their independent commissions such as New Westminster, Hamilton and the others to which I have referred. He has the absolute authority to authorize that work in each one of those harbours. With regard to the national harbours, the bill provides that consent must be obtained from the Minister of Transport, with two exceptions; and they are extremely important exceptions. Of course, this particular feature is very important to me as a member from Vancouver because our harbour is the lifeblood of our whole city. The exception is that the minister can give a letter authorizing a work in the Vancouver harbour without any reference whatever to the national harbours board or to the Minister of Transport. Furthermore, the minister can make regulations of all kinds-apparently even dealing with national harbours

without referring to the Minister of Transport.
I suggest to the minister that he should be unwilling to have himself placed in that position. We do not want him authorizing on his own works for the Vancouver harbour. Certainly they should have the approval of the national harbours board and of the Minister of Transport. But once the Minister of Public Works gives such-and-such a company a letter saying that they can build a pier, and once they go ahead on that letter and start building the pier, it is going to be fairly hard to get them stopped. It is just breaking down the whole chain of authority in that harbour. I hope the minister will agree to make some change in that provision.
I repeat that this appears to be a case where the minister's department is asking for more power than is necessary and, in so doing, is running the risk of breaking down an act which is one of the foundation stones for our water transport in Canada.
This nation will always be much concerned with water transport. The minister himself pointed out what a great difference the St. Lawrence seaway is going to make. Of course, that is true. We have new harbours opening up. I think it was he who just a few weeks ago told us about the possibility of a new harbour up on Ungava bay. We are trying to get harbours in the Alaskan panhandle; we are trying to persuade the Americans that they should let us have harbours in the panhandle on the west coast. I am afraid it is quite a tall order. However, there are going to be these great harbour developments and great developments in the other waters of

Navigable Waters Protection Act Canada, not only on the great lakes and the inland lakes, but also on the seacoast.
Rather than rush this bill through today in the form in which it now stands, I suggest that the minister agree to have another look at it and just see if he cannot propose amendments which will remove these objectionable features of the bill as it now stands.

I do not quite see the necessity for the argument with regard to urgency. I cannot see why this one group of people should be exempted from exercising the normal foresight on occasions when that is necessary.
I, like the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), think the major objection to the bill is that it places in the hands of the minister powers that were formerly in the hands of the governor in council. I base my objections on the same reasons. I can see some conflict of interests, and I think nowadays there is more necessity than ever before for co-operation between departments. What happens if the minister gives authority to build a structure under the Navigable Waters Protection Act and then later it is found that it conflicts with something under the international rivers act? I know that one has to get a licence under that act if the water level is substantially raised at the international border. The minister may give a permit to erect a structure of a certain type without knowledge of the fact that another department is considering raising the level of the water for power purposes or damming a lake or a river. I think, therefore, it would be a protection to all the parties concerned, not only to the government but to the persons who are making applications.
Some mention was made of fisheries. I think the situation as it is today, especially following the introduction of the international rivers bill at the last session and the unusual interest and concern about fisheries, more than ever requires that these applications should be granted as a result of a cabinet decision and not as the result of the decision of one minister.
Now, Mr. Speaker, those are the few brief remarks and suggestions I have to offer. In

my opinion the minister would be wise to have this bill referred to the committee on railways, canals, and telegraph lines, where we could have the officials before the committee as well as other interested persons, and find out what is what. It is a very difficult procedure to understand. Mr. Speaker, I too, listened with a great deal of interest to what the minister said when he moved second reading of the bill and to the observations of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) and the C.C.F. member who has just taken his seat. I also wonder if we are not reaching a point today where we are trying to allocate too much power to a particular minister. I understand that some years ago works of this type were covered by bills which were ratified by parliament before being undertaken. Today we find that more and more, under the guise of urgency, these powers are being transferred to ministers. I believe it is time we had a second look at a lot of these things. The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) suggested the bill be referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines for particular study, after which we could come back with further recommendations.
I would be prepared to support the proposal. I wonder, therefore, if it would not be possible to have a committee composed, let us say, of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters), the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) and the member of the cabinet who comes from the province in which the work itself is to take place. If the minister is going to have to take authority in order to get business done in this house, then it might be desirable
Navigable Waters Protection Act to break it down to the point where at least the province in which the work is to be done has some representation on the committee. It may be that the minister from the province in which the work is to be done may not be particularly interested in that department, but it might give him an opportunity of expressing the point of view of the province on the matter. Now, the great danger as I see it is not only the bypassing of parliament-that was done some years ago when parliament gave authority to the governor in council to authorize this work-but now we are also bypassing the governor in council and giving the minister the right to authorize certain work. I can see a certain danger in this by reason of the fact that the minister may be unfamiliar with the project being undertaken. While on the surface it might seem like a sound piece of work, in the long run it may prove to be quite the opposite. I noticed that in the bill there is the word "substantial" which gave me some concern. On examining the dictionary I found that the definition is, of a considerable amount.
I would say that if the danger to navigation must be of a considerable amount we should know what that amount is. I have in mind, for instance, speaking of bridges, booms, dams, aboiteaux and so on, that there is a certain amount of diking going to waste on the Fraser river, which is a navigable stream. We have reason to believe that the booms in the Fraser river are affecting the dikes, and there is cause for alarm there. Whether or not it is sufficient in amount to have the minister suggest that booms should be done away with, I do not know. I am not satisfied that he has indicated to us what control we would have over the setting up of further booms or dams or any other of these works that are suggested in the bill itself.
In so far as the question of urgency is concerned, I feel very much as did the hon. member for Kootenay West. Certainly, as he suggested, any lumberman or anyone who is thinking of undertaking such a work should have given his plan sufficient thought to be able to give the minister an opportunity of discussing the matter with the governor in council. But I am certainly alarmed at a proposal-and I believe I indicated this earlier-under which we are even doing away with the co-operation through the governor in council that I called for, for instance, in

Navigable Waters Protection Act the building of certain works in my own area, where I suggested that one department was not aware of what the other department was doing, with the result that they were interfering with each other's work.
The fact that the Minister of Public Works should be given this authority is not important in itself, inasmuch as we have a great deal of confidence in him, and share it with others. The important question is whether any minister should continue to have more and more authority delegated to him under the guise of urgency or emergency.

Mr. Speaker, a few minutes ago when remarks were being passed around concerning who was being paid for what, I must say I was wondering whether the Minister of Public Works should not have attempted to have a clause included in this bill which would increase his salary in view of the extra work and responsibility that will be placed on his shoulders if this bill goes through.
Let me say at the outset that as far as I am concerned I can appreciate the desire of the minister to streamline and perhaps

Navigable Waters Protection Act increase the efficiency of processing the applications that are made under the Navigable Waters Protection Act.
I happen to have with me a copy of the June 16 issue of part I of the Canada Gazette and I notice in this particular issue there are notices of 12 applications under the Navigable Waters Protection Act and while that may be somewhat unusual there are nevertheless a good many applications appearing in the Canada Gazette from time to time, certainly since I have been a member of this house.
As I say, I can appreciate that there may be some need for an overhaul of the methods that are being used in processing these applications; however, it does strike me that the range of the types of proposed structures which come within the purview of the Navigable Waters Protection Act is of such vast magnitude, it is a rather difficult question on which to generalize particularly with reference to the matters which have been raised by other hon. members who have spoken on this side of the house concerning what discretion the minister himself should have. I must say that, as I read through the act, that was the question which immediately arose in my mind concerning just how advisable it is to make the transfer which is proposed from the governor in council to the minister.
I can see there are certain types of applications which will be made under this act which may be considerably over the $5,000 that is provided in one place and that could very well be decided directly by the minister without any great danger of anyone being hurt; but at the same time applications are being made under this act from time to time for proposed structures that can have an extremely significant effect upon the area in which they are proposed to be built. I think there is a real question as to whether or not it is advisable under those circumstances to have complete discretion rest with any one minister of the cabinet in a situation of that kind. One of the thoughts that occurred to me is that if this proposal of transfer to the minister is put through there should be coupled with it some provision in the act for an appeal to the governor in council under certain circumstances. As far as I can make out, this bill does not propose that; it leaves complete discretion with the Minister of Public Works, and the only form of redress which any group of citizens would have would be to exert sufficient pressure to force the resignation of the particular minister which would require his replacement by someone who might be disposed to reconsider the decision that has been made. I think

those questions do arise and I am therefore very much in agreement with the suggestion made by my friend the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) that this bill could very well be studied by the appropriate standing committee of the house.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, that when this act is being brought up for amendment there might very well be other matters which could be considered in committee as possible further amendments to the act that are not covered in the present proposed amendments.
I know, for example, that not so long ago a temporary obstruction to navigation was being created near the mouth of a certain river, and while the technical forms with regard to it, concerning notice of the closing of this stream to navigation and so on, were applied, the practical effect was that this stream was closed to navigation without any real notice having been given to those most concerned, those people who were going to be using it. That particular situation comes under another part of the act which is under the direction of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler), but if that sort of situation is being repeated in other parts of the country there might very well be room for a discussion in committee of an appropriate amendment to the act to cover that type of situation. This is one of those cases where notice was given in a paper nominally circulated in the district and, because it happened to be handier to put it in a paper that had very little circulation, that was where the notice appeared and as a consequence of that the people knew nothing about it until the obstruction was actually in place.
Coming back to the bill, at the moment I am interested in the part which suggests that approval may be given to structures which have been in place for five years. I am wondering if that provision will not give approval to a practice which exists already. I can remember seeing a structure put across a navigable stream and after it had been up a couple of months a notice appeared that so-and-so was applying for permission to construct such and such a work. This is another matter which might profitably receive a careful review by a committee of the house.
I think a study might also be made as to whether or not some division could be made in the types and categories of works to be approved by the Minister of Public Works alone and those which would require to go before the governor in council for consideration by the cabinet as a whole.
These appear to me to be some of the considerations involved in the amending bill which would warrant its being sent to a committee for thorough study when we could

have before us the technical witnesses who could deal with the matters involved.

Mr. Speaker, earlier in the session this matter was brought up by me in connection with a project which we had under way and I understood the minister to say at that time that an amending bill would be brought before the house at this session. I am going to discuss the bill only as it concerns my own area as beyond that I could only speak generally.
I think the bill may be criticized justifiably for giving power to one minister, but on the other hand where small amounts are involved I do not think enough discretion is given to the minister. I would refer again to the case I referred to earlier in this session. No matter what part of the house we sit in we are all interested in the economic development of Canada and if there is legislation that retards that development then it should be changed or more discretion given to the minister in order to take care of isolated cases. Perhaps "isolated" is not the correct word to use.
I am going to refer now to something which occurred in my own riding. Within 40 or 60 rods of my home there is a creek which is as wide as most rivers. It drains a great deal of farm land and where the creek empties into lake Huron it is probably 85 to 100 feet wide. After the spring rush of water is over the mouth of this creek fills up to a height of five or six feet with sand with the result that during the summer farm lands are flooded. We grow sugar beets in that particular area.
As I have mentioned on numerous occasions, the sugar beet growers are obligated to ship their sugar beets by train instead of truck in order to prevent the spread of nematode, which has been the curse of the sugar beet industry in some parts of the United States, particularly in Utah. This involves additional expense.
We had a project under way to keep open the mouth of the creek by building a jetty on each side with an "L" at one end which would permit boats to come in and at the same time prevent the sand from filling up the creek and stopping the natural flow into the lake. As a matter of fact the former Minister of Public Works had his engineer in London examine this project and he was favourably impressed, particularly with respect to the agricultural aspect.
In fact this project has been started but it is now at a standstill because they cannot get permission to continue, either under this act or under the previous act. I understand that other projects have been undertaken and completed on lake Erie and no doubt in other areas without the approval of the
Navigable Waters Protection Act minister. In a case like this where a project has been undertaken to build a jetty to keep open the mouth of a creek and where permission was not obtained the minister should be empowered under the act to grant a permit in order that such a project might be completed. In this particular case they cannot get a grant from the provincial government until the project is legalized by the federal authorities, and apparently the project cannot be completed without a provincial grant.
There is another aspect to this project, that concerning our tourist industry. For some time the minister was in charge of our tourist industry and he knows how important it is for us to obtain United States dollars by that means. Facilities would be provided in this particular creek for probably 100 fair-sized boats to lie at anchor in the area provided by the jetty or further up the river where docking facilities would be available. I say without hesitation that that project would mean probably $100,000 a year to that particular area, and when I say that it would mean that to that particular area I mean that it would mean that to Canada as a whole. We should not scoff at $100,000 or more a year.
There is nothing in the act which would enable this project to be completed. It was started a year ago by the township and by the people of the area but they did not obtain a permit. They went as far as they could building the walls going out into the lake but when it came to obtaining a permit it was found that they should have obtained it before the work was undertaken.
This is one of many reasons why this bill should go to a committee in order that the act may be revised to take care of injustices such as this. Correction would mean, as I say, probably hundreds of thousands or even millions of dollars to the economy of this country. The bill is important. In my area I cannot reconcile myself to this situation. The Ontario government has leased a great deal of water area in lake Huron from Sarnia up to Grand Bend and in lake St. Clair and lake Erie. That is all navigable water. If the bill is not referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, then perhaps we can have some explanation of that when we are in committee of the whole because there are hazards so far as navigation is concerned.
I repeat that when people want to undertake a project and it is possible to obtain a provincial grant to complete the project there should be authority under this act or some other act whereby the minister would be empowered to grant a permit in order that

Navigable Waters Protection Act the job can be completed and so that they can get the necessary funds. Private individuals cannot go to the township council or to the provincial government for additional grants because no permit can be granted under the act.
I say emphatically that the act should take care of such cases in order that projects of that sort can be undertaken and completed. We have there one of the greatest areas for the tourist industry in the Dominion of Canada. If we can increase our tourist revenue there and elsewhere in ridings all across the country it will mean that revenue will add up to a billion dollars instead of remaining static at a little over $300 million as it has now for several years, and it really means only about half that amount when we consider that the dollar is only worth 50 cents.
We must be realistic and undertake to develop the tourist industry. If through policies adopted by parliament the government can stimulate the tourist industry throughout Canada it will benefit the whole economy. We will then achieve our objective, but we are not going to do so if we sit back and ignore cases such as this which could be remedied by simply changing the wording of an act. Under the act a permit must be obtained in order to undertake work and yet at the same time I notice, as I emphasized a few moments ago, that even if a work has been constructed illegally approval can be obtained if it has been completed for five years. If you can grant a permit for a work constructed illegally which has been completed for five years, why not grant a permit for work begun last year? This is not a political matter. It is a matter of common sense, and I think we must apply common sense if we are going to get the best out of any legislation.
I hope that the bill can be referred to a committee. I dare say that it affects most of the ridings in the dominion. The standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines is one of the largest committees of the house, having 50 or 60 members, and I think we could get some very constructive ideas from those who would in the meantime give this bill further consideration. Even if we are unfortunate enough not to have the bill sent to the committee, I hope that in the meantime the minister together with his advisers will take upon himself the job of revising the particular section of the legislation which would empower him to grant a permit where work has been undertaken by a township or by responsible bodies and probably only requires two or three months to complete the job. In this one instance, as I say, it will probably mean $100,000 a year


or perhaps a great deal more to that particular area and the same change in the act may mean millions of dollars per year to the economy of the dominion.

I think this bill or one like it should determine what are navigable waters in the minds of the government because up until now they do not know. The Department of Transport will not classify a stream of water as navigable water unless it will take a motorboat or a tourist or commercial boat. I have gone to them about different streams in an effort to get a little work done and they have told me that they were not navigable waters and they would not have anything to do with them.
But when you go to the Department of Public Works they will call them navigable waters if they have enough water to fill a 4-inch pipe. I have a case in my own riding where there is no water for six months of the year. There would be no water at any time except that some 50 years ago a dam was erected to back up the water. But now one of these fellows who wears an iron ring, an engineer, comes and looks at it and classifies it as navigable water. Nothing has ever gone up there except possibly a canoe 50 or 60 years ago. No boat of any kind has been able to go up it since and no boat can do so now except at high water when there is water behind the dam. A boat cannot go there unless they drag it on the ground.
These engineers are clannish, and I give the minister credit. He depends on his engineers and he backs them up when they make wrong statements and form wrong judgments. However, I am probably like the engineers too. I like a fellow who will stay behind me when I am wrong, and that is the way the minister is so far as some of his engineers are concerned. He stands behind them when they are wrong.
Nevertheless, I think you should have some legislation to say what is navigable water and what is not because up until now the minister's department does not know and the Department of Transport does not know. Get your heads together and put something in the bill that will tell us what is navigable water and what is not. The bill should go to a committee because there are several important things involved. I may say to the minister that I had some correspondence with

him about the stream to which I have referred. He wrote and told me that it was navigable water. A child two years old could walk up there in his bare feet in the summertime. There is not one drop of water but still it is classed as navigable water.
The municipality and the provincial engineers put some tiles there to take care of the rise in the water when they put the logs in the dam. The water backs up into a slough. It never was navigable. It was a swamp. The timber was cut off 50 years ago and not a log was ever floated down the stream. An Indian might have gone up there at high water. Nevertheless, your engineer classifies it as navigable water. I wish the minister had the time to go and look at these things himself. He would see how stupid some of his engineers are. That place never was navigable water and is not now. The municipality put tiles there. The minister knows about it. I wrote a letter to him and he still claims it is navigable water.
The municipality will not take the tiles out. You will have to take them out, and part of the act provides for you to take them out. You had probably better send the army up there when you send an engineer to take them out because there is plenty of deep water there even if there is none in the creek.
I like one thing in this bill. It might give the minister a chance to use the telephone. The explanatory note states that the purposes of the amendments are to provide for approval by the minister, and to extend the exemptions. Subsection 2 states that this section does not apply to any work other than a bridge, boom, dam, aboiteau or causeway-I suppose that takes in creek-if, in the opinion of the minister, the work does not interfere substantially with navigation and if the value of the work does not exceed $5,000. This work I am talking about does not exceed $300 and it never was a navigable water and it is not now a navigable water. I would invite the minister up there. I will take him fishing or do anything he wants to do, if he will come up and have a look at it himself.
You cannot fish in that stream, can you?
No; not for crabs. There is not enough water there for crabs or crayfish. There may be a few bugs.
I do not understand all this, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member will have to speak louder if he wishes me to hear him.

I like that part of the bill where, among the exemptions, it provides if the work does not interfere substantially with navigation. That is another reason why this
18, 1356
Navigable Waters Protection Act bill should go to a committee. Then farther down, in section 4 we find these words:
(a)	if, prior to commencement of construction, the minister, having been satisfied that the work was urgently required, consented in writing to commencement of construction; or
(b)	if five years have elapsed since completion of construction of the work;
and such approval has the same effect as is given prior to commencement of construction of the work.
That should be changed to two years. Why do you want five years in it? I know these engineers are fairly slow, but I do not think it will take them five years to look at a thing like that. They could do it in two years or less than two years. Let us make it two years. A great many changes must be made in this bill. It needs a greater opportunity for examination than we are going to be able to give it here in the House of Commons. I would therefore ask the minister to send this bill to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

I just want to ask the minister a question before he replies. I shall be brief. Following up what was said by the hon. member for Victoria, Ont. (Mr. Hodgson) with respect to the definition of a navigable stream, and after reading what is said in the act, may I ask the minister to say whether there are some waters or streams which are regarded as navigable streams controlled by the province, or are all navigable waters controlled by the federal government? If all navigable waters are controlled by the federal government, how do you go about getting from the minister a decision as to whether a certain body of water is or is not a navigable stream? As the minister is no doubt aware, at least in the province of Ontario the question of whether or not a certain body of water is a navigable stream entails certain rights with regard to traffic and fishing. I for one would be greatly interested if the minister, in his reply, would tell us as plainly and frankly as he can just what is a navigable stream.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank all hon. members who have taken part in this debate because I think they have shown the two sides of the question as they exist here. Some hon. members thought that the provisions of the bill now before us go too far whilst others feel that they do not go far enough. Those have been the reasons why the government felt it necessary to ask for amendments to this old statute at this time. The applications are being received at the rate of about 300 a year and that number is on the increase. Most of these applications

Navigable Waters Protection Act are in respect of works of a minor character. One hon. member suggested that it might be wise to form some sort of committee with provincial representation on it. In that regard I would remind hon. members that the majority of applications received are made either by or on behalf of some provincial government. It seems to me that the category that comes before us most frequently is that of applications having to do with transmission lines passing over some navigable water.
I gather that there is no serious criticism of the powers being sought in this amending bill. The question which occurred in the mind of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) and in the minds of others is whether the powers being sought should be administered by the governor in council or by the minister. I can tell hon. members that it is a comfortable position for any minister to be in to be able to refer matters to the governor in council. But that is not always the best way or the most expeditious way in which to discharge the responsibility which is simply, in this case, the administration of the provisons of the act. The governor in council is a committee of the cabinet and not the full cabinet, as some hon. members seemed to think. Another question raised was the matter of urgency.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: How many are members of that committee?
Four constitute a quorum.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: To talk about a quorum is a different thing than to refer to a committee of the cabinet.

Is my hon. friend asking a question or making an assertion? I do not care which it is. It is all right with me. The question of urgency was raised and hon. members rightly queried whether any urgency was great enough to warrant the authority being given without the necessary approval under this statute. We have had some cases where the question of urgency arose. For instance, in the constituency of my good friend the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor),-
That is right.

-last year a main broke under the Kaministikwia river. It was necessary to obtain authority under the Navigable Waters Protection Act to develop an alternative structure to carry the main under that river. With winter coming on it was absolutely essential that that work be put in at the earliest possible moment. There are other such cases. It is true that they are rare. It is also true, what the hon. member

for Vancouver-Quadra has said, namely that we should think very carefully before sacrificing any of the rights on navigable waters.
As to whether or not the federal government has jurisdiction over all navigable waters, I understand that under the British North America Act that is the case. As to what constitutes a navigable water, it is often difficult to decide. There are various means of navigation, and what is navigation in the eyes of the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) and in mine might be quite different from what constitutes navigation on a stream remote from the sea and farther inland. All these rights must be protected. We have places where there are small streams and where people are in the habit of travelling on them from time to time by canoe. We have had instances where farmers have built a fence across a stream, thereby denying other local residents a chance to pass along the stream by canoe. To a seafaring man, that might not seem to be very important navigation but to those people who use it for their ordinary day-to-day activities, it is important. All these things must be considered.
As to consideration by a committee, I know hon. members are aware of the fact that this bill has already been before the other place, that it was considered carefully there in a committee and that it has been referred to us in this house with one minor amendment. We are now about to go into committee of the whole and I am quite prepared to have hon. members ask any questions they see fit to ask. I think they can be assured of the same diligent consideration here by all members as is customary in committee of the whole house.
But witnesses cannot be called.

I would therefore simply conclude by thanking hon. members for the part they have taken in this debate and to tell them that, in my opinion, this bill is the best compromise with regard to a situation that obviously necessitated a change in the face of conditions as they exist in Canada at the present time.
May I ask the minister a question? Do I take it he is unwilling to have this bill go to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines?
I am of the opinion that the necessary consideration can be given to this bill in the committee of the whole house.

Would the minister answer a question? How does his

department ascertain whether or not a small stream or inland lake, whatever it may be, is a navigable stream?

So far as we are concerned in this department, Mr. Speaker, it is a matter of the use that is made of the particular stream and also, of course, the size of it and the potential use that may be made of it. There are a variety of factors, but I would rather err on the side of saying it is navigable than saying it is not navigable if there is any doubt.

Take my	
own district, in which there are hundreds	
of lakes, some	of them perhaps a couple of
hundred miles	around, but which are only
used as tourist	resorts. There is no lumbering there. Would the minister say, offhand,	
if those would	be navigable waters which
would come under this act?

Yes, I would think so, without examining	a particular case. If the lake
or river is capable of navigation, then it	
would come under this statute.

Then, what	
is navigable?
