Bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Apple-whaite in the chair.
On clause 1-Minister.

Mr. Chairman, I was somewhat amazed when the minister in charge of this bill who is at the same time the minister who will be given these very drastic powers, refused to agree to have this bill referred to a standing committee of this house for consideration. One excuse he gave for taking that stand was that the bill had been considered in the other place. I have here the Senate Hansard containing the discussion on the bill, and it occupies about two pages. We have had-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is a full discussion for them.
As the hon, member for Winnipeg North Centre says, that is a full discussion in the other house.
A committee studied this bill.

I presume it went to a committee in the other house, as all their bills do, but I do not believe we have any transcript of the evidence that was taken in that committee of the other house, if any was taken. I very much doubt whether there was a very full examination of the measure, and it is going pretty far when a minister in
5128	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Navigable Waters Protection Act this house says that one of the standing committees of the commons, and a good committee-I call the hon. member for Fort William as a witness to that statement-
I agree with the hon. member on that.

-a good committee should not be given the opportunity to consider this bill. If it had been sent to a committee, then we could have had the Minister of Transport, the Minister of Public Works and some of the other ministers who are concerned; we could have had the deputy ministers; we could have found out just what are the difficulties. But oh, no; this Minister of Public Works, acting in the same dictatorial manner that we are witnessing so often from this government this year, acting in just that same way, brushed aside the request made from every party in the opposition that the bill at least be sent to a committee. He brushed that aside and said "No, we will give it second reading now and then you will have a chance to ask me some questions when it goes into committee of the whole." It is just about time the Canadian people realized what is going on in this house. Here we have a bill which has been on the statute books of Canada for many years, one of the most important bills on our statute books, yet the government is prepared to have the heart torn out of the statute without even having it considered by a committee. I submit that the minister is absolutely unreasonable in his refusal to let a committee of this house consider this bill. Even yet it is not too late for him to change his mind and do that, give the committee a chance to deal with the bill as it should be dealt with. Just to have it rammed down our throats in the way that has been done this afternoon is not good enough.
There are other members who can deal with different aspects of the bill, but I point out to the minister again the situation with respect to the harbours of Canada. It is all right to try to justify this on the basis that some little stream requires a ruling under this act because a canoe is going to go up that stream. It is all right for the minister to put that forward as his excuse for having control of all the operations under the act, but the matters that are really vital under this statute are the multi-million dollar piers and works of that type that will be erected in different parts of Canada. That is where the real issue lies, and the decision on those important works should be left in the hands of the cabinet.
It may be that there should be amendments made so the minor works could be handled by the minister without having them

submitted to the cabinet, but there is no excuse whatever for giving the Minister of Public Works or any other single minister sole power to decide whether or not a million dollar pier is going to be placed in one of our harbours.
That condition may arise in Vancouver, and the Minister of Transport, who has charge of the national harbours board, should be in on that picture, and so should the ministers representing British Columbia in the cabinet. Those questions are too important to be decided by one minister and certainly by a minister from another part of the country who really has very little knowledge of what conditions are to be met, and who cannot be in a position to understand what is reasonable in a port in another part of Canada. This applies not only to the national harbours but also to the other harbours to which I referred.
I have here the annual report of the Department of Transport for the year ending March 31, 1955, and we find the following at page 71:
Harbours Administered by Harbour Commissioners.
There are seven harbour commissions as follows: Belleville, Hamilton and Toronto in Ontario; Winnipeg-St. Boniface, Manitoba; New Westminster, North Fraser and Port Alberni in British Columbia.
And then we find this report:
General supervision is exercised over the affairs of the commissioners and all by-laws are submitted for approval of the department before submission to the governor in council for confirmation. The commissioners make by-laws concerning navigation, rates, tolls, penalties, etc. They also administer water lot transactions affecting federal property within the harbours, the accruing rental forming part of the harbour revenue.
They do all that under the Minister of Transport, yet once this bill has been passed the sole jurisdiction will be with the Minister of Public Works. The Minister of Transport will not have the slightest authority to say anything about this. There is no responsibility to give him any information; there is nothing in the bill to require that, and because it does not go to the cabinet there is no way by which he can know, unless the Minister of Public Works places it before him. Even then the Minister of Transport has absolutely no responsibility, because under the bill all the responsibility is given to the Minister of Public Works.
For the life of me I cannot understand why the government wants to place the full authority in respect of these works-which are really big works, and which may affect the economy of large segments of Canada- in the hands of one minister. I submit that is contrary to our whole parliamentary belief. It is contrary to the way in which the

government of Canada has been run. In my judgment it is just another example of the fact that this government has been in power so long and has such an overwhelming majority, that the members of the cabinet simply have a contempt for parliament, a contempt for the opposition and in effect a contempt for the wishes of the Canadian people.
Once more I urge the minister to withdraw his dictatorial and unfair action in refusing even to have this bill sent to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. It is still not too late for him to do that. That is the proper way in which this bill should be considered, and it is the proper way to have it amended. The bill as it stands today is not right, and I believe there are ministers in the cabinet sitting opposite right now who realize this bill is not right in its present form. The only way it will be adequately amended is if it can be referred to the standing committee.

Mr. Chairman, like the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra I was quite disappointed at the action of the minister in refusing to allow this bill to go before a standing committee of the house because, as I attempted to point out in the few remarks I made on second reading, it struck me as being the type of bill which could very profitably receive the kind of consideration that is possible only in a standing committee, where it is the practice to have such people as deputy ministers appear to answer our questions and give us detailed information concerning the administrative problems the proposed bill is presumably designed to correct.
I think everyone realizes it is difficult for members like myself, who are interested because we live in areas where there are substantial quantities of navigable water, to consider in committee of the whole house amendments to a bill of this type if we are not satisfied that it is entirely as it should be, but in the standing committee we have an opportunity of obtaining more detailed information on the basis of which we can judge whether or not any objections we may have are well founded. For that reason I must say I share the views of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra in this connection.
I do not think there is much more I can add concerning clause 1 of the bill because it simply designates that "minister" means the Minister of Public Works. As I understand it, that designation of the Minister of Public Works applies only to the part of the
18, 1956
Navigable Waters Protection Act Navigable Waters Protection Act which heretofore has come under his general jurisdiction.
I hope that as we proceed, inasmuch as apparently we are not going to have the bill sent to the committee, the minister will be prepared to give us some detailed explanation of the various changes that are proposed.

I just want to add my protest to those of hon. members who have already spoken concerning the fact that this bill is not going to be sent to the appropriate committee.
I think it is one of those little things which, if it were done, would help to remove the frictions that almost inevitably occur in a place like this.
As I read the bill, the main change is the transfer of the authority which previously was in the governor in council to the minister. I do not know whether that is a good or bad thing. Possibly with the present minister in charge of the department it might be all right and there would be no need to worry, but ministers come and ministers go. While we might all be quite happy to leave these regulations under the control of the present minister there might come a time when there was a minister in charge of the department about whom we would not be so pleased. Is the Minister of Finance raising an objection?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: None whatever.

Referring the bill to a committee would not unduly delay it. If anything it would facilitate the other business of the house, because while this bill was being considered in committee the house could be dealing with other business. When the bill came back to committee of the whole it would probably go through with little discussion. I am sorry the minister did not see his way clear to refer it to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. Since he has not done that I imagine the best thing to do is for hon. members to attempt to bring out all the relevant facts while we are considering the bill clause by clause.

Mr. Chairman, the question in my mind at the moment with regard to the bill and the clauses thereof is whether the Prime Minister has so far renounced his control over his cabinet and the affairs of this country that he leaves it to individual ministers to bring in measures of this kind which would redivide or reallocate authority within the cabinet which had previously been held by the cabinet as a whole. As the hon. member who has just resumed his seat pointed out,

Navigable Waters Protection Act one of the cardinal features of this bill is the transfer of authority from the governor in council to a specific minister. The sponsor of the bill is the minister to whom authority is being transferred.
It is a most peculiar and unusual situation to find that the man who has the primary responsibility for the present government and for the present cabinet is not even interested enough in the various responsibilities of his ministers to sponsor or comment upon a radical change of authority within the group which he controls. At the present time we are fortunate in that the right hon. Prime Minister is in the house. To say the least I think it would be appropriate and helpful if he would signify that he also approves of this transfer of authority within his cabinet. Are we going to have from time to time other bills of this nature sponsored by individual cabinet ministers which break down the authority of the Prime Minister, which parcel out among themselves responsibilities which ministers are to have, which grant to ministers authority previously vested either in parliament or in the cabinet? I should like to know whether the Prime Minister approves of this transfer of authority from the cabinet as a whole to this individual minister.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps this will be the only opportunity I will have to refer to a matter I referred to earlier. When I suggested that the minister should be given more latitude and power I did not mean that to apply to projects such as have been mentioned this afternoon. But as I said, with minor things there should be latitude, especially when the project has already been started. In the particular case I referred to they will not be able to get any assistance from the municipal or provincial governments until a permit is granted. Discretion should be with the minister in order that this project may be undertaken.
I am going to ask the minister if in cases like this he will undertake that a permit will be granted. I am not going to repeat the argument I made earlier, because time is valuable; but I mentioned that the completion of this project might bring $100,000 or perhaps several times that amount each year from the tourist industry.
A point which I did not make a while ago is that there will be no cost to the federal treasury. It will run about $10,000 or $12,000 to complete the project, but they did not apply for a permit and they cannot go ahead. They are stymied, the tourist industry is stymied, and the sugar beet growers still have to ship their sugar beets by train instead of by truck, which means additional cost. We do not want

to do anything to handicap the agricultural industry in Ontario. This could be taken care of by a simple rewording of a particular section of the act.
I do hope the minister will see his way clear, not only in the case of this particular project, which is important to this area, but in all such projects that there is some latitude in interpreting the act, or that an amendment is made to make the granting of a permit possible. If this additional revenue came into that particular area it would be of great assistance and would also assist our agricultural economy.
Let me repeat that it is not going to cost the federal government anything. We do want a permit to be granted so the township council can go ahead and complete this project. It may involve $10,000 or $12,000 but it will not cost the federal treasury anything and the return will be perhaps 10, or 15 or 20 times the amount spent. These people are most anxious to have the work undertaken and they are sorry, as I am, that there is no provision under which they may obtain this permit. I do hope before the bill is finalized the minister will consult with his officers and in some way see that authority is granted so projects like this can be finished.
There is one other aspect to this matter which I did not think of when I was on my feet before. As I said, the mouth of this creek fills up to a height of 5, 6 or 7 feet. The Department of Agriculture has some pictures which were taken some years ago when we endeavoured to prevail upon the Minister of Agriculture to do something to prevent the spread of this nematode disease, which is the curse of the sugar beet industry and which is brought about by the flooding of hundreds of acres of farm land.
This is the point I have in mind. Of course I was referring to lake Huron as navigable water, and there has been reference to other navigable streams which are apparently a great deal smaller than the one I have in mind. What is the responsibility of the federal government for damage to property because of the closing of the mouth of this creek? It closed up long before the present project was started, so the fault does not lie in what has been done. However, because there is no protection to prevent the sand from coming in and closing up the mouth of the stream, which is about 75 to 100 feet wide, the farmers are losing thousands and thousands of dollars on account of the flooding of their land. I am wondering who is responsible. Is it the federal government because they are not doing what can be done?

The difficulty can be overcome. All you need do is see that they get a permit to complete the job. This is only one of these instances. It is something that may happen in my riding today and in your riding tomorrow, but I say in all seriousness that I sincerely hope the act can be amended, because there may be many other such incidents. No expense whatever is involved so far as the federal government is concerned. All we want to get from the federal government is the authority to do the job.

Mr. Chairman, like other members who have spoken I regret that the minister has not agreed to send the bill to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines; and I am not taking that position just to be awkward. There are federal and provincial jurisdictions that are related to the bill. I know that in my own district lumber companies that want water lots for booming grounds have to approach the lands branch of the department of lands and forests of the government of British Columbia, advertise, and go through certain procedures. When they have the booming ground they have to drive dolphins and piles to hold their boom chains so they can contain the logs.
There is a lot of misunderstanding as to what is legally necessary in securing these properties, what is under the jurisdiction of the provincial government and what is under the jurisdiction of the federal government. Therefore I think if the bill had gone to the standing committee we would have had the opportunity to listen to the minister's officials and to the legal advisers. There would have been clarification of the relationship, shall I say, between the federal and provincial jurisdictions, and that would have been of advantage to many who are interested in building structures and other things that will come under the terms of this legislation.
Seeing that the bill is not going to the standing committee, I wish the minister would give an exposition to the committee of the procedure necessary under the circumstances I have outlined.
The procedure necessary to obtain approval under this statute for a work in a navigable water? Is that what my hon. friend has in mind?

A work in a navigable water or lake. Here is a company which wants to establish a mill and a booming ground. It gets its water lot from the provincial government. Then it has to drive piles and dolphins and erect other structures to contain the logs for the mill. In some cases the companies, after having obtained the required licence 67509-325
Navigable Waters Protection Act for the water lot from the provincial government, go ahead and drive piles and put in dolphins without any reference to the federal government. In other cases other companies follow the procedure necessary under the terms of the act. Would the minister tell the committee what procedure should be followed by a company-I have some knowledge of what I am talking about-which intends to establish a booming ground and has obtained a licence from the provincial government with respect to a water lot in the area concerned?

They must make application under this statute and submit plans and a description of the site to the Minister of Public Works. Then they must publish notice in the Canada Gazette and in two local papers; and the notice has to be given for a period of a month. Then the Minister of Public Works considers granting the application. That is a simple procedure. There are exceptions provided by this statute in cases of urgency, but generally speaking the procedure is the one I have outlined.
Before the clause carries, would the minister answer my question?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Would the minister not have saved time by sending this to the committee?

I was particularly interested in the question raised by the hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac with regard to what constitutes navigable water, and I must say the explanation the minister gave still left me in some considerable doubt as to what is navigable water. I am particularly interested in this matter as far as streams are concerned, especially where a stream flows through a man's farm or ranch.
I should like to know from the minister whether there is any definition in the Navigable Waters Protection Act or elsewhere in the Transport Act as to what constitutes a navigable stream. Is there a minimum width or anything along that line? In other words, is a small stream 5, 10 or 15 feet wide, which happens to run through a man's fields, interpreted as being a navigable stream because you can push a canoe or a small rowboat up it or even a small boat with an outboard motor? As a result is the farmer in the position that before he can put a bridge across the stream or do anything else along that line in order to enable him to carry on his work, he has to apply to the minister in order to get permission to do it?
So far as I know, this sort of thing has been done on these small streams more or less from the beginning in Canada, but as I read the act it would seem to me that with respect

Navigable Waters Protection Act to such a stream the man would have to ask permission of the minister. He would have to get his consent, file plans and so forth before he even put a fence across the stream, let alone anything else. Would the minister comment on that?

Size is not much of a criterion in determining whether or not a stream is navigable, and I do not know of any specific definition which delineates the navigability of any water. It is generally held that water is navigable if it is capable of being navigated for the trade and commerce of the area. Beyond that, it is a matter of judgment as to whether that is the case. That is the situation.

In view of the minister's last remarks as to the interpretation of "navigable", may I say that I know of areas in western Ontario where numbers of rafts have been put in streams in order to move cement and other things to the other side, and I presume the minister would consider those streams navigable. Before the bill goes through this stage would the minister consider having some of his assistants or possibly someone from the Department of Transport draw up a definition of what a navigable water is, even if the definition is broad, to be included in the interpretation section; because I think more and more this matter will become a subject of public interest and attention. I cannot see any reason why some definition cannot be put in the interpretation clause.

Mr. Chairman, I think we could tell the hon. member for Calgary North that the old swimming hole is going to disappear under this legislation. I would think the minister probably will be making decisions with respect to whether boys can build the necessary dams or whether or not they can be given the authority.
How about beaver dams?

It seems' to me that the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, who said he was surprised at this action being taken by the minister, really was not stating his true feelings about it. I do not think any one should be particularly surprised that this type of legislation is being brought forward by this government. As I see it, this is just further evidence of adherence to the cult of "get things done".
Hear, hear.

Don't applaud too soon over there. As I say, this is just further evidence of adherence to the cult of "get things done", regardless of what happens in the process. What happens to the ordinary
[Mr. Harkness.l
course of parliamentary government does not seem to make much difference to the members opposite.
Nonsense.

At least the committee is perking up, anyway. I heard somebody over there make reference to the fact that we were in committee now, and that is the first sign that we are. Prior to that you were sitting mildly by and you would let any of these sections go by without a word.
In any case, this is just a further indication of the trend that we had last year in the defence production debate. As will be recalled, it was not a case of handing over powers to the governor in council in connection with that legislation, it was a case of handing them over to the minister himself. Here is a further step along the way.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the members to your right have not learned any particular lesson from what happened last year or given any indication that there is some sign left of cabinet responsibility in connection with legislation of this type. I think that is the important thing. If we continue this trend we are going to have a great many individual cabinet members who, it may be said, are responsible to the Prime Minister but who in fact are no longer going to be responsible to this house. If it is the type of government in existence in the United States that you want here, I say we are certainly going a long way down that line; but it is far removed from the principles of British parliamentary institutions that heretofore have been the guiding light for this institution.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that it would not have been too tough for the minister to have differentiated, to a certain extent, between the various types of activities that he is going to carry on here. I note that in one case he has been able to set a limit of $5,000 on the construction to take place and has said that in that case it will be done in a certain way, and that over and above that amount it will be done in some other way. If he intends to acquire these powers himself, surely he could have gone one step further. If it is necessary to remove it from the intricate, day to day handling of things in this house, he could have put some other type of ceiling on the activity where he could have handled it himself, and we could have had some indication then that over and above that figure we would be back in the position of having cabinet responsibility.
After all, that is the way we expect things are going to be done. We cannot examine

every individual item which comes along. But I think we sitting over here in the opposition have the right to expect that the responsibility is being taken by all the gentlemen on the treasury benches, and that it is not being carried on by one man alone. Hence I say that here is a piece of legislation that could have been submitted to the committee.
I might say this. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, when he said he was surprised, may have been surprised because it was this particular minister who was doing this to us. But certainly here is a piece of legislation that could easily have been submitted to the committee. As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, I might say that it would have received there some careful examination from the members on the government side as well. I have found that in committee they have just as many questions to ask as anyone else. It would be a good thing for this legislation to go there to be considered and then receive the stamp of approval of the whole house. But let us not go down this road to which I have referred, step by step. Here again is a place where a check can be put on this type of government. Let us think very seriously about it.

Mr. Chairman, I think one of the things this bill shows most clearly is that you get far better legislation when it is drawn up by a Conservative government than you get when it is drawn up by a Liberal government. The original act stood for 70 years and it evidently pleased everybody. This act that is just being introduced pleases nobody. I think it is obvious that this bill should have been brought before the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines in order to allow it to be examined, in order to bring before that committee the deputy ministers and the ministers themselves, and to let the committee give the bill-one as important as the minister has said this is-a thorough examination.
What this bill does is concentrate power in the hands of one minister. We have become accustomed to this government ignoring parliament. Now the government even wants to ignore itself. It does not even want to examine measures. It wants to have one minister do the whole job. Obviously in matters pertaining to the protection of navigable waters there is one minister who certainly should be brought in on those discussions, and that is the Minister of Transport. He is the one who is primarily responsible for preserving the navigability of these navigable waters.
As a member from Toronto I object particularly to the fact that this legislation gives 67509-325J
18, 1956
Navigable Waters Protection Act the Minister of Public Works the right to say what works can and cannot be built in Toronto harbour. That is now an important harbour and it will be more important in the future. I think it is completely wrong that the Minister of Public Works has the complete say, without consultation even with the Minister of Transport, in an important harbour such as that and in other important harbours across the country, as to what works can and cannot be built.
I think it is obvious that this legislation should be brought before the committee. I am surprised that the minister, who is usually reasonable, has been so unreasonable in this case. It makes one wonder, Mr. Chairman, what is the matter with this committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. It is a perfectly good committee. It is supposed to examine legislation of this kind. But all this government seems to do with respect to this committee is ignore it.
We had an example of that in the last few weeks. The pipe-line bill should have been brought before this committee and examined. The committee was ignored in that case. Here we have a bill which the Minister of Public Works says is one of the most important pieces of legislation we-have. Once again an important piece of legislation is not brought before that committee for examination. What is the matter-with the chairman of the committee? Have' the government no faith or no confidence in him? Do they not think he could do a proper job?
I should like to hear from the Minister of Public Works what his objection is to having this measure properly considered, and why he thinks that an examination by the committee would not be beneficial in this case.
Perhaps I could answer that question by asking the hon. member what he has against the committee of the whole? What makes one committee better than another committee? I know the answer he will give-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. In any event, the decision of the house has been that we deal with it in committee of the whole. I really think we are somewhat out of order in discussing the matter of referring the bill to a committee at this stage. After all, we are dealing with clause 1 of the bill.
The committee can always change its mind.

I simply wish to remind hon. members that this bill has already been before a committee of the other house, where witnesses where heard. This is the second

Navigable Waters Protection Act time that the bill is before a committee, and in my opinion a very good committee. Any questions that are raised can be answered here; so I think it is quite wrong to give the impression that this bill is not receiving adequate consideration by committees of parliament.

The minister has asked what objection I have to the committee of the whole house. It is simply that we cannot call witnesses before this committee. We cannot have the deputy minister or other witnesses whom we would like to call before the committee for examination.

The Senate committee had that privilege.
:Mr. Hees: Mr. Chairman, you do not really consider that committees of that rest home down the hall give any kind of consideration to any measure?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member well knows the rule with reference to the other place, and I think he would wish to reconsider those words.
Perhaps I could adopt the suggestion of the hon. member near me and call it a quiet haven.

Apparently in this committee we are discussing a bill to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act. It seems to me that nobody, including the minister, knows what navigable waters are or can define them. I certainly do not think it unreasonable that the minister be asked to insert a definition or interpretation, whatever he likes to call it, of navigable waters in this bill, so we will know what we are talking about. Apparently that is the situation now; we are talking about something and none of us knows what it is.

As the hon. member for Oxford has just stated, it is certainly essential that we know what this bill means. In order to know what the bill means, we must know what a navigable stream is. It has been said that the C.C.F. party to our left are Liberals in a hurry. I believe the Prime Minister made that statement. I do not think they could be in any greater hurry than this government is now. The time the measure would take in committee would be very small tin comparison to the amount of time that would be saved after it had been considered in committee.
The disease of power seems to be very infectious. We thought the Minister of Trade and Commerce was the only one who was so desirous of having these powers, but apparently now other ministers are coming along-probably it is the result of jealousy-


and asking for these powers. The disease seems to be very infectious. Other ministers are desirous of getting this particular power. I might say to the minister that under the terms of this bill he will have complete power over the St. Lawrence seaway.
No, no.

The reference in the bill is to any rebuilding, repairing or altering. After the seaway is built I presume some day it will have to be repaired, rebuilt or altered. The terms of this bill would give the minister charge of that part of the seaway.
I have the honour of representing a riding which includes the most of the Grand river, or a far greater percentage of it than any other riding. I presume the Grand river is a navigable water, so it seems that the minister could rip out any dam or tear down any of the things that are there now and would not have to ask permission to do so.
The hon. member for Calgary North mentioned a small stream running through a person's farm. I have a small stream running through my farm. I would not consider it navigable, but there are parts of it in which a canoe could be floated. There are other streams that I am sure could be considered navigable which run through farms, and does that mean a man could not put a line fence across the stream without getting the minister's permission? It would also mean that the minister could come along and tear down that fence if it were put up without his permission. A neighbour could complain that the fence had been constructed without permission and have it torn down.
There are many farms on which it is necessary to put a bridge over a stream in order to get to the farm buildings. Does this mean such people would have to go to the minister to get permission to build a bridge? It seems ridiculous. If the minister would give us a logical reason why he wants all these powers it might be different, but he has not given us that logical reason.

I do not like to keep pressing this point, but I think we are entitled to an explanation from the minister as to why he will not put in the bill some definition of what the word "navigable" means. If all these extra powers are to be given to the minister, it certainly seems sensible to me that some definition or explanation should be inserted in the bill as to what the word "navigable" means.

I did not intend to get into this debate at all, but a question now arises in my mind as to the river Thames. I have always understood that it

was navigable as far as Chatham, but I am wondering whether you are going to include London, and if so if you are going beyond London to the Fanshawe dam. What effect is that going to have on the water resources committee of the province of Ontario? I think this is rather hasty legislation and we should know a little more about it before we are asked to pass it.

I wonder if the minister could tell us if he knows of any court judgment that may have been rendered with regard to waters being navigable within the meaning of the act. I have in mind this. I was wondering what the proceeding would be, for instance, if some person on a stream erected some work and another resident of the district objected to it on the ground it was being erected in navigable waters. Presumably if that were the case, after having appealed to the department to give some ruling, if the minister gave the same answer that we did not know what navigable waters were, then presumably that person would have recourse to the courts to prevent these people from doing that. If that were the case, would the department play any part in that litigation? Would they have representatives there? Is there a case in which the department has had to get a court judgment with regard to whether or not a stretch of water comes under this act?

In my relatively short
experience with this statute I know of no case in which we have actually been in court. I understand there is one pending now in western Canada, in which the department ruled that a certain structure could not be built over a stream because it was navigable. This is being contested, and I would imagine the officials of the department would appear if the case is taken to court. It has not yet been taken to court, but I understand that is being given serious consideration.

I do not want to say very much, but I do know that if we had had to wait for a cabinet meeting in Fort William it would have cost Fort William many dollars. Money is just as valuable up there as it is in Ottawa. I was going to ask the minister how many cases he had dealt with in the past year. I think he said there were 300, all under $5,000.
No, I would not say that. There have been over 300 applications, and a number of these exceeded that amount. But most of them were for small projects.

I do not think it necessary, no matter what the opposition says, to call a cabinet meeting to spend $300 or $400 on a
18, 1956
Navigable Waters Protection Act small project. The government would not do very much else if they had to call a cabinet meeting for each of these applications.

I think the hon. member for Fort William is under a misapprehension as to what we are saying. We are asking that this bill be referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. I suggest to the minister that during the dinner hour he might look up an old case of which I have a faint recollection, because we must have a definition of navigable water before we can pass this bill. There is an old case. As I recall it-the river Thames was mentioned a few minutes ago-one of the litigants was Williams, and it concerned the river Thames and its navigability above Chatham. It concerned the taking of gravel two or three miles above Chatham at a place called Kent Bridge. That was supposed to be the end of the stream's navigability. Whether that case would help I do not know. It certainly sounds like common sense to me.
When the bill was discussed in the house the hon. member for Victoria (Ont.) expressly stated that in his riding there was a little stream the water of which is now being carried down by two tiles; yet the minister's department calls it a navigable stream. It may be navigable for muskrats to run races in. How can we accept that as a navigable stream? It is beyond my comprehension and I am sure it must be beyond the comprehension of all hon. members in this house.
We must know what is a navigable stream. Is it a stream going through a farm? As has been said here, it is going to be necessary for the farmer to get permission from the department to build a bridge or to build a line fence. The thing is ludicrous until we know what the definition is. Surely the Department of Justice, or the legal advisers in the minister's department, can tell him what a navigable water is so we shall have it on the record. We are dealing with a very important subject, and until we know what the definition is we should not be asked to pass this bill in its present form. Before this bill passes the minister should give me an answer to the problem that is being faced in my particular riding.

I have already said that to the best of my knowledge the definition of whether a water is navigable is if it is capable of supporting navigation in the interests of the trade and commerce of the area. There are many local factors that enter into that. Surely hon. members do not think there is a hard and fast definition that has to do with a cross-sectional area of the stream, the speed of the current or any of these other

Navigable Waters Protection Act matters. I am told by the legal people that that is the generally accepted definition in law, whether or not a stream or a water is capable of supporting navigation in the interests of the local commerce of the area.
As to the other question raised by the hon. member for Lambton West, the situation there is that the structure has been started. It was started without an application under the Navigable Waters Protection Act, and there simply is no authority under the statute to grant a permit. It is a matter for judgment on the part of the local officials as to whether they wish to finish the structure they have already started without seeking approval, but there is no authority in the statute to grant approval until the period of five years now being sought elapses.

Mr. Chairman, just on that point, I am very glad the minister has gone that far and said that the authorities can proceed with the project. The unfortunate part of it is that they have gone into it without getting any help from the provincial government. It is definitely understood that they can go ahead and get private subscriptions and even grants from the municipal council to complete the project?
It is a matter for the exercise of local judgment in that respect, sir.
Judgment of the council, I assume?

Mr. Chairman, in view of what the minister has just said as to his interpretation of what a navigable water or navigable stream is, how is any farmer, or any other person, in that situation to know whether he is at liberty to put a fence, a bridge, or any other structure across a stream which flows through his place? It seems to me that still leaves the thing in a very unsatisfactory state. With these thousands of small streams which exist in this country and which flow through people's farms, and so forth, it seems to me those people should be in a position to know whether they can carry on their normal operations which require bridges, fences, and so forth, or whether before they do anything they have to go to the expense of preparing plans and sending them in to the minister and then perhaps waiting a long time to get a decision and never knowing really where they are. Can the minister say that the provisions of this act generally speaking do not apply to those thousands of small streams which run through farmers' fields, and so on?

I cannot give any blanket statement such as that. The hon. member for Broadview said this was good legislation

and that it stood the test of time for 70-odd years because it was prepared by a Conservative government. I imagine the tests of navigability over the 70 years have been very much the same as they are now.
There never has been any attention paid to this before.
Yes, there was, to the extent of 300 applications a year.

Another matter has come to my attention. What position would a person be in who was about to use water from a stream for irrigation purposes? It could interfere with navigation because it could lower the stream, as it has lowered streams in many instances around my own district. There has been considerable controversy about the use of this tremendous amount of water for irrigation in instances where people put in small dams to make pools on a small stream. I believe there is a case in court now having to do with whether or not it is right for a person to put a dam on a small stream. What is the position of a farmer if he takes water out of a stream, and some of these large irrigation trunks take a lot of water from streams? They lower the stream quite considerably with a 4-inch or a 6-inch line. What position is he going to be in? Is he going to have to go to the courts to find out first and prove to his own satisfaction whether a stream is navigable before he can stick an irrigation pump in it?

Under this part of the act the Minister of Public Works is concerned with structures. The bleeding off of water which changes the level of the stream, perhaps, is not related to the structures at all, and the Minister of Public Works would normally have no jurisdiction in that connection.
Well, the work does not interfere substantially with navigation.
Is it a work, though; is it a structure?

Mr. Chairman, I am glad the minister has left the definition of water in small streams in a way which satisfies me. He said he was willing to leave it to the judgment of the municipality in which the stream is located to say whether or not the stream is navigable. I think that is fair. I think that is a good idea.

I do not think anything I said can be construed in such a way as to give it that interpretation. If the municipality decides that a stream is not navigable and wishes to put a structure on it without first obtaining approval, then it is up to it to take

the gaff if at any subsequent time the local citizens decide that their rights of navigation are impaired. It is a matter for local interpretation.

In the case of the structure, if it did not affect anyone from the common sense point of view, was not an obstruction but was helping 10 or 15 people, would you not take the municipality's judgment in that case?
It is a question of whose ox is gored. There are courts to decide that problem.

Nobody's ox is being gored. The obstruction is on what you call navigable water, but the municipality says it is not navigable water and the province says it is not navigable water. Your department says it is. It may be a stream only 2 feet wide, and no boat ever went up there larger than an Indian canoe which may have gone up there 50 years ago. Nothing has gone up since. There has never been a log floated down the stream. In a case of that kind would you say that your engineer was right and that it is navigable water even though the municipality and the province say it is not? There is no obstruction to anybody, but it is giving benefit to a whole group of tourists who want a road in there, and who put a 16-inch tile in the creek. What is your decision on that?
What is my decision? I do not think it is before me for decision, Mr. Chairman.
If you cannot make a decision now it will have to be made by a judge in Toronto, because the municipality will never lift that tile.

It is obvious the minister has approached this problem in a rather lighthearted manner, and he is now finding out that this is a serious proposal which he is putting before us. He should have accepted advice and had this matter discussed in a standing committee of the House of Commons where officials could have been called in and questioned. He proposed to do it in this manner, however, and he is not gaining any time by so doing.
The minister obviously has launched on a course of empire building. He wants his own little empire now. It has become the standard practice of the members of the cabinet, particularly those who are looking ahead. The minister must establish a position so he may rank on a level with other members of the cabinet who are inspired by similar thoughts.

He has not the
highway to link it up yet.
18, 1956
Navigable Waters Protection Act

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

Perhaps the difficulty with the trans-Canada highway has caused him to divert his attention to something else which he thought he might slip through the House of Commons on Monday afternoon without any attention, but we are going to examine this empire and see just how solidly based it is.
It seems to me incorrect for someone to come along here, as is done from time to time, and say, "Now, for ease of administration it is better to make just a slight change, and here you have section 1 which is merely a modification of the interpretation section of the act; let it go through". When you look at it closely you discover that the modification of the interpretation section of the present act makes a major change in the existing act.
Now, why is that change necessary? Has the minister informed us? Has there been something wrong with the administration of the act over the last 70 years, or is there some other reason? No change should be made in the statutes of this country unless there is some good reason for that change. Has the minister put forward any good reason on this occasion? Not that I have heard yet, except the somewhat plausible excuse that for ease of administration it is better to have these matters under the Minister of Public Works.
If you examine the act closely you will discover that is not a good reason to advance. This act affects more than one minister. As has already been pointed out, the Minister of Transport is affected by part II of this act. When two ministers are concerned it is reasonable that the cabinet as a whole should take matters into consideration. Someone else has already pointed out that works done under this act affect provincial jurisdictions. There again I think it would be very important that the cabinet as a whole, which gives representation by area, should be apprised of any major works that are going to be undertaken under this particular act.
It is for these reasons, in my opinion, that the act was originally drawn up in its present form, so the cabinet as a whole could examine the proposals brought forward. All the ministers of the crown were given an opportunity to give their advice with regard to the proposals rather than having it rest with just one minister. I see no reason to make a change at this time. In matters of the magnitude of those covered under the present act I think the governor in council is the proper body to deal with it.
The Minister of Public Works, if given the authority he desires here, might engage in

Navigable Waters Protection Act construction over navigable waters that would interfere with plans of the Minister of Transport, who is responsible for keeping channels of communication open. You would have a conflict of interest there that would be difficult to resolve. That would not necessarily arise if in the future, as in the past, all projects were examined by the cabinet as a whole.
When you look at section 4 of the present act you find the minister has a certain limited responsibility. The framers of the act in the past had enough common sense to see there were minor construction projects, minor alterations and so on, that should not come before the cabinet as a whole, and the Minister of Public Works has that power already. While I think that is a fairly satisfactory arrangement, it could be modified at the present time to make allowance for the change in the value of money.
Those who framed this act had a fairly good idea of what was required in dealing with navigable waters. I am sure they must have examined the whole situation not only as it relates to the small stream, but the large river and the great lake as well. They must have said, "These are matters which should be the concern of the cabinet as a whole," and they must surely have considered that when great and expensive bridges were being built or large canals were being constructed or altered, the cabinet as a whole should give consideration to the matter. Millions of dollars might be involved in these projects. Why should the responsibility be given to just one minister?
When other ministers and jurisdictions are concerned the obvious place for the authority to rest is	with	the	cabinet	as	a whole.
Consequently the minister is making a mistake in coming before us with a bill of this nature, slipping in a little phrase to the effect that in section 1 "minister" means the Minister of Public Works, and asking us to put that into the interpretation section and then proceed. It is not going to be done quite so easily.
The minister is under obligation to inform this house	why	this	change	is	necessary.Why is he	doing	this? Why	does he want
this power? In the future what will be the difference that will result from this proposed change? If the proposed change is incorporated I think trouble may arise in the future as the result of giving so much power to the Minister of Public Works.
The minister	has	given	no	adequate
explanation of his reasons for wanting this change. He has not looked far enough ahead, and the house obviously is not convinced. Has the minister considered the implications

of placing in his hands the construction of million dollar enterprises, giving him the job of deciding whether or not they are adequate for the purpose for which they were constructed? Is he the one to determine alterations in connection with the St. Lawrence seaway in the future or in connection with any of the great projects across Canada? Is he the one to decide where and what bridges shall be built in the future? Is he the one to decide what shall be done concerning the navigable waters of the northern reaches of Canada as civilization progresses further north? Why just this one minister?
Of course, if the minister lives forever and continues in office forever-
Heaven forbid the latter.

-there may be some people who would say this is the man who could make a sensible decision; but people on this side of the house living so closely in companionship with the Minister of Public Works are not so sure he is either going to live forever or stay in office forever, or that he is necessarily equipped with the capacity to make decisions of this magnitude.
I suggest also to the minister that he change clause 1 and strike out the small alteration he is trying to slip into this act, and leave the direction of the Navigable Waters Protection Act to the governor in council. The cabinet as a whole should decide on these vast projects. The Minister of Public Works should be given authority over the smaller ones which come within the ambit of this act so the cabinet would not be overburdened with decisions. With the cabinet dealing with these matters the Minister of Transport would be protected with regard to his responsibilities and other jurisdictions would receive adequate protection. As it stands the bill is unsatisfactory.

I should like to ask the minister if he does not honestly think that the member of the cabinet who would be in the best position to know what would or would not impede navigation is the Minister of Transport. Does he not honestly think the Minister of Transport should have charge of this act?
Mr. Chairman, on that point I would again refer to the long-entrenched position which the hon. member cited earlier.
Even Conservatives can make mistakes.

Mr. Chairman, I hope you heard that. That has been the situation since the dawn of time so far as this act is concerned. These applications have always been processed through the Minister of Public

Works because the Department of Public Works was one of the first departments established, in fact it was in existence before confederation. Whether that practice should be altered, I do not think I am the one to say. 1 am simply saying that has been the practice for years, and to the best of my knowledge it has worked satisfactorily. We are seeking no change in that procedure now.

As I say, even after 70 years perhaps this Conservative act could have some changes made in it. If the government is going to make changes in this act, I am asking the minister if in his opinion it does not seem logical, because it does seem logical to me, that if you are going to have to make decisions 300 times or more a year as to whether certain buildings, docks and things of that kind will impede transportation, is not the Minister of Transport in the best position to do it because he understands what are the navigational requirements of certain streams and rivers. What we are trying to do is make a good, sensible job of this act, and I am asking the minister, in all seriousness if in his own mind he does not think that is so.

As hon. members know, the Minister of Public Works is responsible for the construction of all wharves, breakwaters, skidways, groynes and thousands of other protection works, with certain exceptions. A great many of these applications have only local importance, being of interest to fishermen who navigate in the area and so on, and in that field I think the Department of Public Works has acquired more experience than perhaps any other department of government. I am not trying to convince hon. members that the Department of Public Works is the only department which can properly do things, because I do not believe that is true, but in this instance I consider it is appropriate that the Minister of Public Works should decide whether these structures will or will not impede navigation.

The original act has stood the test of time for 70 years, and under the original act the Minister of Public Works had to bring these measures before the whole cabinet. In the cabinet there would be discussion in which the Minister of Transport and all other ministers whose areas might be concerned would participate. That provided a definite safeguard.
Does the minister not think that rather than these decisions being made by him and his department, certainly in connection with the larger projects the decisions should be made in co-operation with the Minister of Transport, who would have a greater knowledge of what should or should not be 67509-326
Navigable Waters Protection Act allowed in the way of obstructions? There should be a requirement that the Minister of Public Works should obtain approval from the Minister of Transport in connection with projects costing over a certain amount.
I quite agree that the smaller projects could be handled by the minister and his department, but I think the Minister of Transport should be brought in on these discussions. For instance Toronto, in which I am particularly interested, will be a most important harbour once the St. Lawrence seaway is developed, and I certainly would like to feel that the Minister of Transport was looking over all projects having to do with wharves, buildings and things of that kind before they were given the O.K.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

At six o'clock, Mr. Chairman, I was asking the minister, since the act is being changed by the bill so there is no requirement to bring these measures before the whole cabinet and they can be decided by the one minister alone, whether he did not consider that it would be better to have these decisions at least made by the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Transport, because the Minister of Transport should know more about the requirements of navigability than the Minister of Public Works. I would appreciate it if the minister would give me his opinion and tell the committee if he does not think the two ministers together should be in consultation on at least the major projects, rather than the minister alone.
I am sure the hon. member is aware that there is cabinet solidarity here-
Since when?

-and that every minister who acts on his own responsibility is not apt to do anything that is inconsistent with the responsibilities of any other minister. I think he can take it that the minister, in the exercise of his judgment, is certain to canvass all other ministers who have an interest in the particular subject or who are in a position to help. I can assure him that would follow automatically.

There are one or two other matters concerning which I should like to ask the minister for an answer. First of all, how is this control going to be exercised in

Navigable Waters Protection Act so far as rivers are concerned which come under the International River Improvements Act passed last year? Those rivers are primarily the Columbia river, the rivers running through the panhandle of Alaska, and the Saint John river.
As I understand it, that act is under the administration of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I have a copy of that act here, and I believe there is no mention of the minister of that department in the act itself. Powers are given to the governor in council in the same way they were given to the governor in council under the existing Navigable Waters Protection Act. Regulations under the International River Improvements Act are to be made by the governor in council, just as they are at present under the Navigable Waters Protection Act.
The bill before us now will make a difference between the two types of work. The International River Improvements Act will be under the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources for administration but the regulations will be made by the governor in council, which I think is the way it should be. However, under the Navigable Waters Protection Act the Minister of Public Works will have all the power and in addition he will have the power to make regulations. Incidentally, I notice that the act reads that he will have power to make regulations for navigation purposes, which just shows how ridiculous it is to have the Minister of Public Works in charge of the Navigable Waters Protection Act, the main purpose of which is to protect navigation. I think the act should be administered by the Minister of Transport.
Will the minister explain what will happen on these international rivers? Suppose a company wants to build a dam or a pier on the Arrow lakes to cost say a million dollars. I think the Kaiser dam was to cost $2 million. Under the proposed amendments to the Navigable Waters Protection Act the Minister of Public Works can say whether or not the dam is to be built. I presume they would then have to go to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources under the other act. Will the minister explain just how this is going to be worked out?
I give this illustration to show that it would seem to me to be much wiser to have the authority given to the governor in council. Then the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources and the Minister of Transport could be sitting in with the Minister of Public Works and all the ministers affected could make the decision.


My second point has to do with harbours, first of all national harbours and, second, harbours where there are independent commissions. Will the minister explain how works to be erected in these harbours will be permitted and just where the Minister of Transport fits into that picture?

These are all matters of cooperation among the various ministers concerned, and just because a statute does not specifically say that an application has to be referred to a committee of the cabinet does not mean that the members of the government concerned do not consider it and consider it very fully. Generally, as this statute points out, the jurisdiction of the Minister of Public Works is limited to the navigational aspects of structures in navigable waters, and when the Minister of Public Works has authority by this bill to make regulations for navigation there is the limitation that he can only make regulations for navigation purposes respecting any work to which this part applies.
With respect to international rivers, this statute will apply as it has applied heretofore in the case of structures that are being built and are likely to have any bearing on navigation, just as on any river that flows entirely within our national boundaries. There is no problem there. We have been discussing with the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources the general application of our various jurisdictions, and those talks are still going forward because we want to have it clearly understood in both departments just what our responsibilities are.
With respect to harbours administered by the national harbours board, if there is a structure to be built an application is made under the terms of part I of the Navigable Waters Protection Act, and it is processed through the Minister of Public Works just as the act presently provides.
But then submitted to the governor in council.
Heretofore it has been submitted to the governor in council. The change here is that the minister will have the authority now, but the procedure is still the same apart from that.

The procedure is the same apart from the power to make the real decision, which at the present time is held by the governor in council. By this bill that power of deciding is being taken away and placed with the Minister of Public Works. Is that not a fact?

To this extent, that heretofore the decision was submitted to the governor in

council on the recommendation of the minister and now the decision is to be made at the ministerial level. The reason for that is the multitudinous number of these applications deal largely with very small projects. They are usually matters of transmission lines over streams and the like. It seemed to the government that a more reasonable and expeditious way to handle them was for the minister to assume the responsibility and have the authority that goes with it.

Why not divide these applications? The minister has said several times today that there are quite a large number of applications. It would be very helpful if he could break down the number and tell the committee how many there are in each category. In the last annual report of his department for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1955, there is the following at page 13:
The number of applications made for approval of the plans and sites of works in navigable waters pursuant to the Navigable Waters Protection Act, the Railway Act, the Pipe Lines Act and special statutes continued to increase with 225 applications being processed during the fiscal year. Two licences for the operation of international ferries were issued.
That refers to four different types of operations, one under the Navigable Waters Protection Act, a second under the Railway Act, a third under the Pipe Lines Act and a fourth under special statutes. The bill we are considering today only deals with the first group. Can the minister give us a breakdown of what those numbers are and then a further breakdown giving the types that have been made under the Navigable Waters Protection Act?
I think nobody objects to the minister himself dealing with minor applications. There is no controversy about them. What we are worried about are the big applications which really matter, where there is a large amount of money involved or where a structure is of great importance from a navigational point of view. For that latter group we think it is wiser to retain the control in the governor in council. Can the minister give us a breakdown showing how many are in each category?

Speaking from memory, I
would think that much less than 10 per cent of the total number of applications made are of any significant size. The rest of them are rather matters of routine processing of applications which have to do with small structures; largely they are in connection with the spanning of streams by transmission wires. That is what constitutes the general run of applications.

Why not leave the power in the governor in council to deal with this 10 per cent which are really important and vital, and let the minister take the power to deal with the smaller ones? Would not that be the reasonable way to do it, rather than to give him complete jurisdiction over all these applications, no matter how large the scheme may be?

It is very difficult to try to break them down on a dollar basis. Sometimes a smaller structure such as a bridge which might cost only $200 or $300 might have a most important effect on navigation whereas, conversely, a very expensive structure might have a relatively small effect on navigation. I might say that we have considered some such delineation, but it just did not seem to be practical because there is no way of breaking down on dollar value and saying that just because something costs a great deal of money, its effect on navigation is important.

But in the bill the minister himself has made a division. In the new section 4 he has differentiated between a bridge, boom, dam, aboiteau or causeway and the other works. Why could there not be a breaking down on that same basis of the powers exercised by the governor in council and by the minister?
On that point, may I say that is a matter of policy, Mr. Chairman; and the government felt that the responsibility for making the determination should be vested in the minister.

Just in order to get clear in my own mind how this act will be worked, I have a question to ask. For instance, the minister knows that we hope there will be some extensive developments on the Columbia river within a few years. In the meantime, suppose some company or some person comes along and wants approval for a certain work. Then later suppose the raising of waters or something of that sort covers this work or floods it. Does the minister give consideration to a situation like that as a result of consultation with the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, so this person or corporation would not get approval to build a certain work now and then have a claim say in four or five years against the crown or the authority building a dam or raising the waters, or against even a private company doing the same thing? Are these matters investigated?
Very much so; yes.

Mr. Chairman, I think some of the answers we have just received from the minister in reply to some

Navigable Waters Protection Act of the questions he has been asked further substantiate the argument we have been making, namely that this legislation should have been sent to the committee. I want to continue on that line for just a moment. It seems to me that almost every clause in this bill contains some type of technical wording. I would think the only place where we can possibly get the answer from the [DOT]experts-that is, the experts over and above the minister-would be in a committee.
I know I am not supposed to refer specifically to the items that are contained in the legislation, but I might say that, in connection with the clauses, I see wording like this: We have added the word "altering," making the phrase "rebuilding, repairing or altering". It would be interesting to know why this type of wording is required as an addition in a section of this kind. Perhaps we shall get the answer from the minister, but I say that in all likelihood it is something that should be explained by those experts in the department who have had something to do with drafting the legislation itself.
Further, I notice that we use the term "substantially" in the phrase "the work does not interfere substantially." Here again we are placing in the hands of the minister some very great power. He alone is going to be *the person who will make the decision.
Farther down in clause 4 we find the words '"that the work was urgently required". Here is another term that I defy almost anyone to define, certainly from the legal standpoint. These words, Mr. Chairman, are all in addition to the words "navigable waters" which I notice have been referred to in legal cases but have been shoved aside very quickly when it came to giving judgment, so that little attention has been paid to the actual definition of the words themselves.
Then later on we have the words "if in the opinion of the minister, the interference with navigation..." That is another very technical term in connection with this legislation; I refer to the term "interference," and the fact that the minister is going to take upon himself the whole power to determine whether something constitutes "interference".
And last, there is a technical point I think in the last clause of the bill dealing with the question of the minister making orders or regulations for navigation purposes in connection with this act; and then the fact that the governor in council may make orders and regulations for purposes affecting navigation if it emanates from any other act of the parliament of Canada. The question there is as to which would be the superseding authority.
All these words remind me of a case during the period of the wartime prices and trade
]M!'. Hamilton (York West).]
board regulations in which the term used in the legislation was "prices reasonable and just". I know the supreme court of Ontario in that case said that they just were not subject to definition. Yet here in this type of legislation we find at least five or six examples of terms which have wide ramifications, and in which we are allowing one man to make the decision as to what they actually mean. Mr. Chairman, I would respectfully request that even now it is not too late for this legislation to be referred to a committee where we can really get down to it and find out what it means.

Before the dinner recess we were trying to get from the minister a definition of what is a navigable stream or a navigable water, and I had referred to a case that I thought was in 1910 or 1911. As a matter of fact it was in 1908, and it happened to be in the area in which I was living at that time and it concerned the river Thames. I think it is important for us to have a proper interpretation of what is navigable and what is not navigable on the record so there will not be any doubt in our minds, and we are the ones who are passing the bill. I certainly do not know what is navigable, and I doubt whether any member of this house knows what is navigable.
This was a case on the point. I just want to read two or three sentences from the evidence in this particular case, which concerned a dispute between two farmers about taking gravel from the bed of the river, and apparently there was also the question of a crown grant in the centre of the river or to the bank. What I am concerned about here are two or three references. This is in the case of Williams v. Pickard, found in 17 Ontario Law Reports, 1908-09. This was a judgment reversing the decision of the divisional court.
Held, reversing the decision of the divisional court . . . that the northerly boundary went to the centre of the stream.
I mention that, and continue:
The main question is whether this description gives the grantee to the middle of the stream, or only to the bank.
Then this struck me in a casual glance at this case:
Then, coming to the question, why should the crown reserve the bed of this river-all the land beyond the post?
That is one of the descriptive points.
History, as well as the evidence in this case, gives a very sufficient reason. The navigability of the river Thames up to the forks-now the city of London-has always been in contemplation, and it has always been known that to make navigation, at all seasons of the year, reasonably practicable, the construction of weirs and locks, dredging and embanking, would be necessary;

Then I come to the next to the last paragraph:
On the question of the navigability of the river Thames, I desire to guard against being considered in agreement with the trial judge in his finding. That that river is navigable for some distance, and to some extent, is too well known to require any sort of proof. It is not needful, in this case, to consider whether it is navigable at the place in question:
That is the point at which the lawsuit involving the gravel arose.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that this house should know and have on record a definition of a navigable stream. We have heard about streams going through farms and all that sort of thing, and none of it has been refuted. I would contend, as an ordinary human being with some understanding of the problems we face, that such streams could not be considered navigable. This is important legislation and I think it is very important that the members of this house, as well as the people of this country, know what is navigable.
