The minister has said, and I think quite correctly, that there is no definition of navigable water. Surely his department must have some method of deciding what waters are navigable and what are not. Are there not some rules by which his department acts? How do they decide whether a water is navigable? Do they send out an engineer in each case to decide whether a particular river or lake is navigable, or is there any rule as to what type of vessels must be used on the water? Are there any rules at all?
It depends on the local situation, Mr. Chairman, and each particular case is examined on its own individual merits.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 2-Application.
Would the minister explain the need for the addition of words "or altering".

This is the result of what was an obvious defect in the act as it stood. Under the old statute we had authority to deal with repairs and rebuilding, but we had

no authority whatever to deal with alterations. With respect to many of those structures already existing in navigable waters there was need for alteration. It became a matter of legal definition as to what was a repair, what was a renewal and what was an alteration. We were caught in the middle, and what we are doing here is correcting what was, or what seemed to us, an obvious defect.
I understand from the minister, then, that this contemplates an addition to an existing structure?
My own concept of it is that it would almost always be in the nature of an addition to an existing structure.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 3-Construction of works in navigable waters subject to approval of minister.

Mr. Chairman, why is this distinction made in clause 3 between a bridge, boom, dam, aboiteau and causeway and the other works which are defined in the definition clause of the original act? They include wharf, dock, pier or other structure, tunnel or pipe, or telegraph or power cable or wire and the approaches or other works necessary or appurtenant thereto, or any work, structure or device, whether similar in character to the foregoing or not, which may interfere with navigation. On what basis did the department pick out these works-bridge, boom, dam, aboiteau or causeway-and leave out at least some of the others which would seem to be just as important and just as likely to impede navigation?

It was considered from our experience, Mr. Chairman, that these were the sort of structures that have been most apt to interfere with navigation. We endeavour here to broaden the exceptions. Under the old statute certain exceptions were specifically stated. Now we are saying that unless the work in question is a bridge, a boom, a dam, aboiteau or causeway, then the minister may deal with it without going through the formal procedure that is prescribed in the statute.
Does that not have the effect of making it unnecessary, for example, for a pipe-line company to comply with the terms of the act in putting a pipe-line across a river?
No. I am quite sure it does not make it unnecessary, Mr. Chairman.

That is not included in the definition of bridge, boom, dam, aboiteau or

causeway. It would seem to make it very easy for them to get by without following the act.

I have a couple of questions that I should like to ask in connection with this clause. First of all, to satisfy my curiosity I should like to know what an "aboiteau" is; I do not know.

An aboiteau is one of those structures that are frequently found in Nova Scotia. It is a development from the old Acadian days when the marshes were drained. It is a structure provided in a dike to allow the tidal waters to run off the marshes; then the gate closes automatically to keep the sea water out.

Mr. Chairman, the minister
forgets that in quite a few of these applications under this new bill there will not be any advertisements at all. The minister is taking the power here to make the decisions himself without any advertising being required whatever in all cases where he believes the work will not interfere substantially with navigation. The word "substantially", by the way, is an entirely new provision in the bill. Formerly the act read "interfere with navigation" and now the word "substantially" is put in. That was obviously put in as a protection for the people who are going to erect these obstructions.
The bill also refers to instances where, in the minister's opinion, the value of the work does not exceed $5,000. In those cases there is no need for advertising at all. If the minister decides in favour of allowing the obstruction the man who is affected by that obstruction has absolutely no rights whatever. He may not know a thing about it until permission has been granted.
I do suggest that this amendment improves the bill, giving the opportunity to appeal to the governor in council. I do not believe the power of decision should ever have been taken away from the governor in council as is being done in this bill, but if it is to be taken away from the governor in council and put in the hands of the minister alone surely there should be an appeal to the governor in council. After all, there are still a few rights left in this country, and surely there is no reason why the person affected by these decisions should not have the right to appeal.

Mr. Chairman, in reply to that I simply say we are making no change from the provisions of the present statute which says, in section 4, subsection 2:
The provisions of this section do not apply to small wharves or groynes or other bank or beach protection works, or boathouses, if in the opinion of the Minister of Public Works
(a)	they do not interfere with navigation, and
(b)	do not cost more than one thousand dollars.
That $1,000 is being raised to $5,000 but the principle is the same. There was no appeal there and I submit no appeal is necessary here.

But the minister is again overlooking the fact that on all the other applications where the minister does not exempt them from advertising the governor in council has nothing to do with it and there is no right of appeal whatever. This amendment will give the right of appeal in both cases; in the first place, in cases where there has been advertising and the minister has decided against the person who wishes to appeal, and in the second place in this other group of

applications which is now much larger than it could have been under the original act.
The exemptions under the original act were very limited. They applied only to small wharves, groynes or other bank or beach protection works, or boathouses, if in the opinion of the Minister of Public Works they did not interfere with navigation. The minister has now slipped in the word "substantially", which of course gives him that much wider power to rule in favour of an applicant. The other provision concerned the $1,000. There is a very big difference, because under the new bill all sorts of obstacles come under subclause 2 with the exception of bridges, booms, dams, aboiteaux or causeways.
I do suggest again the amendment improves the act. In all fairness to the people who are going to be affected by the decisions made by the minister alone there should be the right of appeal to the governor in council.

Surely that is quite a change from the situation under which the governor in council came into the picture where any work was of a value in excess of $1,000.
I think there has been a bit of carelessness in the drafting of this clause. It looks

to me as though those who drafted it tried to recast what is already in section 4 of the act. Apparently they felt that some of the wording had to be carried over. Section 4 of the act as it now is reads:
4. (1) No work shall be built or placed in, upon, over, under, through or across any navigable water unless the site thereof has been approved by the governor in council, nor unless such work is built, placed and maintained in accordance with plans and regulations approved or made by the governor in council.
The point I am making is that in the old section there is a definition of regulations; regulations are spelled out as being regulations approved or made by the governor in council. But the amended clause will read:
4. (1) No work shall be built or placed in, upon over, under, through or across any navigable water unless
(a)	the site and plans thereof have been approved by the minister; and
(b)	tne work is built, placed and maintained in accordance with the plans and the regulations.
I ask the minister to tell us what is the meaning of the last two words in subclause 1 of the new clause 4; I refer to the words "the regulations".

I would refer the hon. member to clause 6 which reads:
Tne minister may make such orders or regulations as he deems expedient-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Does the minister suggest
that the general power of regulation under the act covers the reference in what would be section 4 to "the regulations"? It seems to me that those words are just left hanging in thin air. Actually the stipulation set out in the amended clause 4 does not hang together; it does not have any meaning or any reference. I feel that what happened is that at the request of the minister somebody has redrafted the old section 4 and tried to take out the requirement of reference to the governor in council, and in so doing has emasculated the clause until it does not mean anything at all.
All it now says is that the minister is the boss; if it is above $5,000 he has to approve; if it is below $5,000 he just has to say, "It is below $5,000 and it does not interfere substantially with navigation," and therefore he does not even have to approve.
Unless it is a bridge, boom, dam, aboiteau or causeway.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings says, "Unless it is a bridge, boom, dam, aboiteau or causeway." The only conclusion one can draw from that exception in subclause 2 is that if it is a bridge, boom, dam, aboiteau or causeway it does come under the exception and is therefore one of the works the minister has to approve.
Navigable Waters Protection Act We are given just two choices. Either the minister approves it or the minister tells us that he does not have to approve it.
That is not right.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The minister says that that is not right, but I would be glad to have him explain it. Perhaps I had better put the rest of section 4 on the record so it will be there:
(2) This section does not apply to any work, other than a bridge, boom, dam, aboiteau or causeway, if in the opinion of the minister
(a)	the work does not interfere substantially with navigation, and
(b)	the value of the work does not exceed five thousand dollars.
My contention is that this clause means that if the value is in excess of $5,000 or if it is a bridge, boom, dam, aboiteau or causeway, the minister has to give his approval. If it is anything else the minister simply indicates that he does not have to give his approval. In either case it is in the hands of the minister. It seems to me that it is a bad clause in the first place, but it would be improved to some extent by the amendment which has been proposed by my colleague.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to deal with the question of how the amendment applies. The minister has given an explanation in connection with this clause, but it strikes me that under some circumstances there might be quite an advantage to the minister if there were some form of appeal from his decision. What the minister says about notice having to be given and there being an opportunity for anyone concerned to raise objection is perfectly true; nevertheless if the minister has made his decision, even though there might be some objection, as far as I can see it that is it.
As I suggested earlier, the only redress open to anyone would be to get rid of the Minister of Public Works who was holding office at that particular time, but that might not necessarily be the most desirable thing to have happen for the person who was involved. He might think that otherwise the minister was a fairly good Minister of Public Works, but if he refused to hear the objection raised in a particular situation or, on the other hand, if he listened to the objection that was raised and turned it down, then where are we left? I presume the matter could be raised on the floor of the house by a member of parliament, but parliament might not be sitting for a period of months and then there would be no court of appeal.
One reason in the back of my mind for proposing this amendment is the experience we had in British Columbia in connection with appeals from decisions of ministers, or there
5148	HOUSE OF
Navigable Waters Protection Act not being any such appeal. I am thinking of the situation which arose in connection with the issuance of forest management licences. I do not recall all the details of that situation, and if I did I would not take the time of the committee to relate them. I do know there was a great deal of heat generated in British Columbia over this question with respect to whether or not the minister should have the right to turn thumbs down on a particular application for a forest management licence, and if proper machinery had been set up in the first instance for an appeal from the minister to the governor in council the matter probably could have been settled with a good deal less heat and to the better satisfaction of all concerned.
I still feel that some such provision in this legislation would mean a greater degree of flexibility in its application to some situations. A situation requiring an appeal might arise only once in five or ten years, but the very fact that there was provision for some appeal from the decision of the minister might in itself work toward a satisfactory solution without the necessity of anyone having to resort to an appeal. I really wish the minister could see his way clear to accept a proposal along the lines I have suggested.
Amendment (Mr. Barnett) negatived: Yeas, 27; nays, 59.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I declare the amendment lost. Shall the clause carry?

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Kootenay East was good enough to send me over a dictionary to help me out, but it really does not help too much in defining the word "substantially". The minister is going to have some dandies to deal with when this goes through. I wonder how he is going to define the word "substantially".

I have not the benefit of a dictionary before me, but I would think there would have to be real interference with navigation before the word "substantially" would apply. It could not be just some imagined interference. It would have to be demonstrated that there was real interference, and that is why the word "substantially" was inserted.
Is there any particular definition of real interference?
I have no definition of that, Mr. Chairman.

There is one other matter I should like to bring to the minister's attention in connection with clause 3. Subclause 2 exempts certain works from having to have
(Mr. Barnett.]

formal approval. Am I correct in understanding that not only under this bill but also under the old act those works which are exempt from being required to have formal approval do not have to be advertised before they are built? If that is so, I raise the question whether it might not be desirable to have some provision whereby some form of public notice would be given of the intention to construct such works.
The works which have to be advertised are published in the Canada Gazette. Everyone interested enough to peruse the columns of the Canada Gazette is aware of the fact that applications are being made, and those who read their newspapers also know. Inasmuch as the act has been opened, I wonder whether it might not be desirable to have some provision, perhaps not as formal as that required for larger projects, for giving public notice of the intention to construct such works so that if anyone had any objection to their erection or was of the opinion that they would interfere substantially with navigation they would have the opportunity of expressing their views to the minister before the works actually came into being. Would the minister give consideration to that suggestion?

I think that is quite a good suggestion. I have been discussing that very point with our officials and the law officers, and while we have not worked out the means of doing it we do intend to inform the public of the granting of approvals in all these instances.
I should like to make an appeal on behalf of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. There appears to be a conflict of dictatorship here. This bill mentions-
Order.
-pipe lines, and I suggest that is a matter that is reserved for the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The Minister of Public Works has no business butting into pipe lines.
The hon. doctor, who has become a gem of purest ray serene tonight, has uttered words of wisdom which I shall be glad to keep in mind.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 4-Removal of unauthorized works.

Clause 4 writes a new section 5 into the act, and subsection 2 of that section 5 seems to be an entirely new principle in the Navigable Waters Protection Act. It reads:
The minister may, subject to deposit and advertisement as in the case of a proposed work,

approve of the plans and site of a work after construction thereof has commenced
(a)	if, prior to commencement of construction, the minister, having been satisfied that the work was urgently required, consented in writing to commencement of construction; or
(b)	if five years have elapsed since completion of construction of the work;
and such approval has the same effect as if given prior to commencement of construction of the work.
A great many of these works will not even require the formal approval of the minister because they will be exempt under subsection 2 of section 4 of the act once this bill has been passed. What number of cases are there which require this urgent action? As I read this provision, it is not even necessary for the applicant to file a plan. It certainly is not necessary for him to do any advertising before the minister gives a letter authorizing that the work be commenced.
What are the types of works for which this great speed is required? Where quick action of that type is taken, where a short cut of that nature is used, surely the Minister of Transport should be brought into the picture, because the effect of the work is to interfere with navigation. Why is provision not made there that these things should be done with the consent and approval of the Minister of Transport? It is bad enough to provide for the minister to write these letters and thereby permit the construction of the work without the time taken to advertise and without the people who are going to be affected knowing anything about it. As I say, that is bad enough. But surely it is just as bad to keep the Minister of Transport out of the picture. If there are to be these emergency cases, then the Minister of Transport should be brought into the picture.
Actually, under the new section 9 he must be appealed to; he must give his consent in the case of a work in a national harbour, except under this very subsection 2 of section 5. I cannot understand why he should not be brought into the picture not only on a work in a national harbour but also in connection with any other works where this short cut is being taken.
I can assure the hon. member that where the interests of the Minister of Transport are concerned he will certainly be brought into the picture.
Why not say so in the act?

There are not many cases where this will apply, but where it does it is generally a matter of urgency. I think this is one section that badly needs to be inserted in the act in order to give it a measure of workability which it now sadly lacks. There are structures pending now
Navigable Waters Protection Act that cannot be approved because they did not get prior approval, yet they were matters of great urgency. I can think of one that came to us through the channels of the Railway Act which, of course, is administered by my colleague the Minister of Transport. There is another one pending in Vancouver itself.
What is it?

I am not sure of the details now, but there was a structure started there without prior approval. No matter how meritorious that structure might be, we have no authority whatever to give it approval. I know my hon. friend recognizes what that can mean to financing and other development in the area. The fact of the matter is that it cannot now be an approved structure. Under the old section there was no provision whatever for approving an unauthorized structure unless it was built or in course of construction on the 1st day of June, 1938.
The government does not believe any structure should be started without prior approval; but there are extenuating circumstances sometimes, where it becomes necessary because of the urgency of the situation. This legislation does provide for approval subject to the applicant conforming to all the provisions of the statute. By publishing notice in the Canada Gazette and two other papers and going through all the procedure he can then qualify. But in the meantime approval can be given him to proceed with the work.
That is only after the work has begun.
If he cannot qualify, however, the work will have to be undone.
Has there ever been a work taken down after it has started?
Yes.
Where?

I can think of one in the province of Quebec in my time, and I have no doubt there were others before my time. The hon. member for Broadview pointed out how far this statute goes back. I think he should be checked on that point too. But if a structure now goes forward for some reason or other without authority, then five years later the owners of that structure can come to us and say, "Will you consider this for approval?" This section in the statute gives us the authority to do that. In five years its merit or otherwise should be demonstrated. I think this is one section that badly needs to be inserted in the act.

There are two types of works. I should like to deal first with the latter

Navigable Waters Protection Act group, the group the minister has just dealt with. Does he mean to say that a company can put in an unauthorized work, then use that work for five years with nothing to be done about stopping them or removing it, and that at the end of five years they get approval? That is the line of the argument he is making.
Not exactly.
What is the sense of that? The applicant can put in this pier and use it for five years.
Not if it is a structure that interferes with navigation.
He can use it for five years anyway, apparently. Then as long as he gets approval after five years, he is all right.
In the meantime, if it interferes with navigation it falls under another section of the act and he can be required to remove it.

Then the other branch is the case where he has not commenced the construction but where he comes and gets a letter from the minister before starting construction. For the life of me I cannot see why there should be such great urgency in that case. They cannot build a pier or they cannot build a bridge without getting their plans made. Under the act the only delay is that they must give one month's notice of the deposit of the plan and they must advertise in two papers.
But I am sure my hon. friend will recognize that there may be a case where a water main breaks. That has happened.
That is right.

And in replacing the water main it was necessary to have regard to the navigational aspects of the river under which this water main was carried. It was simply impractical to wait one month to replace the water main. Some prior approval had to be given. It happened in the area of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Perhaps I can give my hon. friend a case in point. He is familiar with Vancouver harbour. The Alberta pool wanted to put an extension on their grain elevator there.
On what?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
On their grain elevator on Burrard inlet. My hon. friend knows the locality. The extension could not possibly interfere with navigation. It is back parallel to the shore line. The dock lies out there 200 feet in front of it. Nevertheless,

that structure was built on a navigable water and they had to get a permit under the Navigable Waters Protection Act. Under the old machinery it takes something like two months to get a permit. The fact that the work had to be delayed until the permit was obtained has prevented us from using the elevator probably for the last month. Obviously a case such as that could be dealt with by the minister under this act, whereas it could not be dealt with in that way under the old one.

That may have been a case in which this provision would have come in handy, but that is just the way in which you make bad laws, namely by passing them in order to fit particular cases. The delay under this act is only a matter of 30 days; one month's notice in the Canada Gazette and two publications in the local paper.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes; but you must send the plans down from Vancouver.
Surely anybody who might be affected is entitled to at least that much notice.
What about the case of a water main?

As far as the water main is concerned, under the new subsection 2 of section 4 they are not obliged to get approval at all because they can be exempted under the powers the minister is given there to exempt them.

No. The cost will exceed
$5,000 in every case.

The trouble is that in order to meet one or two cases the minister is putting through a bill which takes away the rights of other people to protest and to have a hearing in respect of these applications.
Not at all.
That is bad draftsmanship and it is bad practice.
That is not the case.

I suggest that this business
of the minister simply writing a letter to the effect that they can go ahead and start to build their elevator or build their water main without first having complied with the law again is showing a disrespect for parliament and for the statutes of this country. It is belittling parliament, and is just in line with the course this government has been following right throughout the present session.

I do not see how you can
come to that conclusion.

There is no use trying to convince the government. I have seen what has been happening here all during this session. Some day the Canadian people are going to catch up with the government and stop this kind of thing.
If the Canadian people have catching up to do on a section such as this, I certainly will welcome it.
The Canadian people who are affected by these works, and whose rights may be affected, are entitled to be given notice and to have an opportunity to be heard.
They have.

Here the minister is writing into the law a statute under which a work can actually be commenced without anybody being given notice, and actually without the minister himself having seen the plans. I submit that is entirely wrong. It is a case of just helping out some friends or somebody who wants to get on in a hurry, and let the other people who may be affected take their chance or lose out entirely. It is the wrong type of legislation, but I am not surprised that the government, in its present state of thinking, is bringing in amendments of this type.

I just want to refer to clause 4, subclause 2, paragraph (b) which reads as follows:
If five years have elapsed since completion of construction of the work-
I know in my own district there are quite a number of small structures, dolphins, piles and so on, that have been driven throughout the years without any authority whatever. I suppose that has happened on other rivers in Canada. It is understandable in view of the circumstances that existed years ago. Now, what does the minister do, shall we say, to legalize all these works when this bill is passed? Are the minister's officials instructed to investigate in the district and ask these people to make application to regularize them, or is it just left as it is? Do they have to bring this matter to the attention of the minister or the department? What is the procedure to regularize these illegal structures?
The onus is on them if they wish to have their structures made legal structures. It is up to them to take action, otherwise they run the risk of having to remove them.
There are penalties under the act for illegal structures?

Yes.

I am a little puzzled about this subclause 2 (b). What is the purpose in having this five-year period after the completion of construction? Why should an application not be made immediately, or as soon as the department is aware that certain construction is under way? Why should they not be required to apply immediately and publish notice in the usual way?

I do not believe the other sections of the statute would have any effect if people were allowed to go ahead and build structures without getting approval, and then subsequently upon application, receive approval. If anybody does build a structure without proper authority, then he must be prepared to wait five years. That is part of the penalty he must pay for building an unauthorized structure on a navigable water. Under the old act, if he built it subsequent to June, 1938, he could not get approval in any event.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 5-Deposit of plans with minister and registrar of deeds.

Clause 5 covers the new sections 7, 8 and 9. The new section 9 reads as follows:
In the case of a work in any navigable water under the jurisdiction of the national harbours board, a reference in this part, except in paragraph (a) of subsection 2 of section 5 and in section 10, to the minister shall be construed as including also a reference to the minister having the administration of the National Harbours Board Act.
Why should the Minister of Transport not be consulted and his consent required before one of these urgently needed jobs is undertaken? For example, I am thinking of the extension of the Alberta pool elevator in Vancouver harbour. The Minister of Transport is responsible for the administration of the national harbours board. All these great harbours of Canada are directly under his jurisdiction. This section is admitting, in effect, that in so far as national harbours are concerned the Minister of Transport should be consulted and his consent should be obtained. Why should it not be obtained in the case where the rules are to be thrown aside and the consent given by letter? Why should the Minister of Public Works be authorized to give a letter in respect of a work in one of the national harbours without getting the consent of the Minister of Transport?

I think it is idle to assume that the assent of the Minister of Transport would not be obtained. The hon. member seems to think this is a balkanized government, whereas there is great cohesion in it

Navigable Waters Protection Act as he, I am sure, knows. Before this section was drafted in this form there were long discussions among the officials of the Department of Transport, the officials of public works and the officials of the Department of Justice. I myself had discussions on this very point with my colleague the Minister of Transport. I can assure my hon. friend on something about which he seems to have doubt, that there is the very closest liaison between members of this government. I can assure him of this, too; that in any matter in which the Minister of Transport is interested his prior approval will be obtained before approval of any structure is granted under this statute.

The Minister of Public Works is writing into this section that the approval of the Minister of Transport must be obtained for any work in a national harbour, which is quite correct. But then, he puts in the exception that such consent is not necessary where it is one of these urgently required works.
1	suggest it would be more necessary in a case like that than in the construction of ordinary works under the other provisions of the act.
Here an exception is being made and permission is going to be given to start construction of a work without advertisement or without notice to anybody, and the Minister of Transport is not asked about it. He is not required to give his consent. I suggest to the minister that those words should be taken out, "except in paragraph (a) of subsection
2	of section 5 and in section 10." Why is it that the Minister of Transport has to be consulted in every other case where there is a work going into a national harbour except where it is being done under the urgent provisions?

I am not clear on the import of the last part of the hon. gentleman's question. I think we have protected the situation here. We do not go beyond what the provisions are now. These matters are considered very carefully. We have the greatest regard for the interests of navigation. As I said this afternoon we intend to see that they are protected. There is no giving away. It is not easy to get a permit under the Navigable Waters Protection Act. All the steps must be taken and all the interested parties must be consulted. I can assure my hon. friend that will continue to be the case.

The minister, for some reason or other, has written into this new section now that the Minister of Transport must be consulted with respect to all works to be put into a national harbour, with the exception of a work which is put in under the urgent

provision. Let us go back to the case of the extension of the Alberta pool elevator in Vancouver harbour. Why should the Minister of Transport not give his consent to that short cut being taken? He has to give his consent if it is done in the regular way; that is, the plans are filed and advertisements are published. Because of the way the section reads now he does not have to give his consent if the minister simply writes a letter and says, "You may start construction". Why should his consent not be required?
It is simply to give initial approval, Mr. Chairman, to start construction, subject to his being able to qualify through the regular channels once that initial approval has been given.

Mr. Chairman, just before the clause carries, I call the minister's attention to subsection 2 of section 7 at the bottom of the preceding page. I am wondering about the draftsmanship of this subsection. I am not now discussing the merits of the bill. The subsection reads:
Where there Is no registrar of deeds for the area . . .
I think the registrar of deeds is an individual rather than an office. This refers to a person, but when you look at the explanatory note you see that it refers to an office, to the office of the registrar of deeds. This subsection says:
Where there is no registrar of deeds . . .
Frankly I think this is draftsmanship the minister should scrutinize pretty carefully. The explanation is obvious. It says that this applies to the Northwest Territories, and that the plans shall be filed at Ottawa. But when you read the section you find that it is general and I suggest ambiguous. It says:
Where there is no registrar of deeds for the area in which the work is proposed to be constructed-
I think it would have been better to say "Northwest Territories" and be done with it. I continue:
-the duplicate of the plan thereof and the description of the proposed site shall be deposited in the nearest land titles office established under the Land Titles Act.
The explanation says that means it is going to be filed in Ottawa. I would suggest to the minister that there are numerous land titles acts in effect in various parts of Canada, and that there is considerable ambiguity in the drafting of this subsection. Perhaps the minister should give it pretty careful consideration before it finally goes through, because when you read the explanation it is very plain and very obvious. If the explanation had been made in the subsection there would be no trouble about it at all. As it reads at the moment I do suggest that some

day there could be a great deal of trouble with the land titles act of Alberta, or of Saskatchewan, for instance. I presume it refers to a federal act. I think it should be scrutinized and possibly amended before it finally passes.
I shall be glad to do that. I am not an expert on legal draftsmanship. I will have it scrutinized and if a change is required it will be made when the bill receives third reading.

I should like to point out to the minister that in subsection 1 he uses the words "may deposit", and in subsection 2 he uses the words "shall be deposited". I understand it is compulsory that the plans be deposited, but apparently the wording-
It is the same wording as the old statute. It has been taken out of the original act.
I know it is the same wording of the old statute. Certainly the words "may deposit" leave in my mind some doubt as to the interpretation being compulsory.
I shall look into that.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 6-Regulations.

Mr. Chairman, clause 6 requires some explanation. Under the act as it stands at present all regulations must be passed by the governor in council. This new section 10 provides that the minister alone can pass regulations under part 1 of the act, but it leaves power to the governor in council to pass regulations with respect to all plans and sites which are approved under any other act of the parliament of Canada. Will the minister explain the basis for that division?

Well, Mr. Chairman, there are regulations required under some other statutes such as the Railway Act, and there are one or two others where the establishment of regulations by the governor in council is required. We are simply stating in this section that those provisions stand as they are, but that for the purpose of part I of the Navigable Waters Protection Act the regulation may be established by the Minister of Public Works.

That seems to be going very far. The minister is given the power to make the decisions under this act. Surely it would be only reasonable to require him to submit the regulations to the governor in council for approval. Instead of that, because of the way this amendment is worded the minister himself not only makes the decisions but he also makes the rules.

I submit to the Prime Minister that that is not right. If there are to be regulations under this act and the minister is to be given all these very wide powers, surely the regulations should not be made by the minister; they should at least be made by the governor in council. I do suggest this section should be amended accordingly.

I am quite prepared to accept that suggestion, Mr. Chairman, and I would ask one of my colleagues to move that this particular section be dropped and that the section stand as it is in the old statute.

speechtext:
Is the
minister going to make a statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: VETERANS BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO GUARANTEED LOANS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is any point in my making a statement. At the resolution stage I explained fully the purpose of the amendment and certain observations were made by hon. members opposite. I gathered from those that they were in complete agreement with the purpose of the bill.

maintopic: VETERANS BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO GUARANTEED LOANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, despite what the minister has said, if he looks back in Hansard he will find that at the resolution stage he said that of the many questions asked some would be dealt with on second reading. I had hoped that when the minister spoke on second reading he would answer many of the questions that were asked by various members at the resolution stage.
As the minister will recall, when we were at the resolution stage members from all
5154	HOUSE OF
Veterans Business and Professional Loans parties in the house generally expressed their approval of this amendment and spoke strongly in favour of the benefits that had been conferred on veterans under this act. Various requests were made to the minister that instead of bringing in the amendment that he is now making the whole act should be extended for a period of 5, 8 or 10 years. On that occasion the minister stated, as reported at page 3295 of Hansard:
It would not be our intention to extend the time unless there are very good reasons for it.
The minister recalls the debate at the resolution stage. Many reasons were advanced why the act should be extended. The minister was questioned as to whether or not it would be necessary to have any further staff and whether there would be any further expense if the act were extended, and he said no. He also agreed that the act would be in force-or at least the administrative sections would be in force-for a long time to come in order to collect the loans that had been made and to take care of the applications that had been made by veterans of the Korean war and by other veterans who are now serving in the armed forces.
It would perhaps be interesting if the minister would tell the house how many veterans would be affected by this amendment. By that I mean the number of veterans apart from Korean veterans who are not really affected by the amendment because their 10-year period has not run out.
According to the report in Hansard the minister gave the impression there had been only one application not dealt with because the 10-year period had expired between the date the application was made and the date the loan was granted. I think the minister will find there have been many other applications, because in the report of the Department of Veterans Affairs he will see there have been well over 7,000 applications. I believe in the last year reported there were somewhere between two and three hundred applications.
As one hon. member pointed out at the resolution stage, applications for assistance are still being received under the Veterans' Land Act. In view of that it seems only reasonable that this act should be extended for a further period of time.
There were other points raised. One was the question, which I thought surely the minister would answer, concerning a veteran of the Korean war who stayed in the army. Let us suppose the Korean veteran was to be discharged in 1958. Does that mean he will have 10 years from the date of his discharge in which to apply for assistance under this act? I ask this question because the


parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs said he may be entitled to it. I do not know whether he used the word '"may" intentionally, but at page 3297 of Hansard the parliamentary assistant is reported as saying:
. . . he may become entitled to the benefits of this act because this act says "ten years after the date of discharge".
He then goes on to state the matter is now under discussion.
There is the other case, Mr. Speaker, of a Korean veteran who is discharged, later re-enlists and serves for a further period and is then again discharged. From what date would his 10-year period operate? Would it be from the date of his first discharge or from the date of his second discharge?
I have several questions here which I wish to ask the minister and I hope he will be able to give us the information. The first question concerns the total number of applications made to date under this act.
Second, the total number of applications that have been refused by the bank, and the number of applications that have been refused by the minister or his officials.
Third, the total amount loaned to date, the total amount that has been repaid, and the total amount that is in arrears at the present time.
Fourth, what is the amount paid by the department to the banks to date to cover losses, and what is the total amount written off as bad debts as of this date?
Fifth, would the minister tell us if there have been any prosecutions under section 10 of the act? If there have been any prosecutions, what is the total amount of the fines paid by veterans? I would also be rather interested in knowing the amount of the largest fine paid by any veteran.
Sixth, under section 11 of the act, whereby the minister may take over the loan from the bank, how many such loans has the minister taken over? What recovery, if any, has the minister been able to make?
Seventh, would the minister be able to tell us approximately how long it takes to process a loan of this nature? Could he also tell us if all the chartered banks share fairly equally in the distribution of these loans, or are there only two or three of the chartered banks which handle the majority of these loans?
In conclusion, I would again appeal to the minister to very seriously consider the extension of the administrative section of this act.

Mr. Speaker, there is just one point I should like to place before the government, arising out of the fact that this Veterans Business and Professional Loans Act is in effect the joint responsibility of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Veterans Affairs. The Minister of Finance, of course, deals with the guarantees to the banks, but the Minister of Veterans Affairs is responsible for deciding whether or not a veteran is qualified. For example, section 4 subsection l(i) provides that:
The application for the loan was concurred in before the loan was made, by the Minister of Veterans Affairs or his authorized representative as defined by the regulations.
And then section 8 provides:
The governor in council may on the recommendation of the minister-
That is the Minister of Finance.
-and the Minister of Veterans Affairs make regulations for any purpose for which regulations are contemplated by this act-
And so on. Section 12 of the act provides:
The minister may pay any amount payable to a bank under this act out of unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund and the minister and the Minister of Veterans Affairs may pay any amount necessary to meet the expenses incurred in the administration of this act out of moneys appropriated by parliament for the purpose.
Just how they decide who is to pay which I do not know; but in effect this is a joint act.
I believe I must protest again tonight, as I did in speaking in the throne speech debate on January 23, 1956, that Canada still has a Minister of Veterans Affairs who is holding two portfolios. I think that means adequate justice is not being done to the veterans of Canada. The Minister of Veterans Affairs was asked about this at the Canadian Legion convention in Vancouver a week ago today; at least the report from which I am reading was published a week ago today. I am reading from the Vancouver Province of June 11, 1956:
Asked from convention floor if the government was going to restore Mr. Lapointe to a single portfolio in the cabinet, the minister-who recently became Postmaster General-assured the convention that the additional duties have in no way interfered with his responsibility to the veteran.
Now, I am not criticizing-

I have in my hand from the Journals of 1949 the ruling of Mr. Speaker in which he is discussing what is and what is not relevant when an amending bill is before the house.
I shall read just a part of it from page 237, as follows:
On the second reading of an amending bill-
Hon. members will notice that this is an amending bill.

it is the principle of the amending bill, and not the principle of the act to be amended, which is the "business under consideration". The discussion must therefore relate exclusively to the principle of the amending bill.
If I may paraphrase, that principle is that certain loans shall be made if application has been made within the time limit, even though the loan was not made at the expiration of the time limit. I think I must ask hon. members not to broaden this discussion to the administration of the Veterans Business and Professional Loans Act, and certainly not to the administration of the Department of Veterans Affairs, which criticism and discussion I think would be much more appropriate under the departmental estimates.

speechtext:
I submit that this amending bill has to do with applications for loans, and part of the process of getting through an application for a loan is to get the approval of the Minister of Veterans Affairs. I submit that I am in order in dealing with the fact that the Minister of Veterans Affairs is only a half-time minister so far as this department is concerned. That is one reason there has been so little veterans' legislation come before us this session. I think this bill and perhaps one other-I am not sure whether there was one other-represent the only veterans' legislation brought before this 1956 session of the house.
I place the blame for the failure to appoint a full-time Minister of Veterans Affairs directly at the door of the Prime Minister. It is his responsibility to see that these portfolios are properly manned. If he were giving leadership to this country as he should be doing he would have had a full-time Minister of Veterans Affairs appointed a long time ago, or he could perhaps have relieved the present Minister of Veterans Affairs of the necessity of looking after the portfolio of Postmaster General. I repeat that this situation is unfair to the veterans of Canada, and it shows a lack of leadership on the part of the Prime Minister.

The hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac read out so many questions that it was impossible for me to make notes in


order to answer them, but I think I should answer generally the points he raised and then perhaps he can ask other questions or he may accept some advice from me about them. The purpose of this bill is to provide a beneficial amendment which will permit persons who have applied for the benefits of this act but whose applications were not dealt with by the time the 10-year period elapsed to obtain the benefits of this act.
When I spoke at the resolution stage I said that I knew of one case only to which this amendment would apply, but I assumed that there would be others in future because of the fact that the 10-year period had not elapsed in every case. Since April 26, when we discussed this last, there have been three more cases come to my attention, so that at the moment the amendment will apply to four veterans. Presumably there will be others.
A general discussion about the act itself, how many applications have been made under it, how much has been advanced, how much has been received and so on, seems to me to be somewhat out of order. Even if it were in order I would point out to my hon. friend that just recently I tabled in the house a report on the operations of this act for the year ending March 31, 1956. That report which is made annually contains full information about the loans made in each year. That report is before the house and would be available to the hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac.
I doubt if I could give any more information than would be contained in the report, but if there is a particular case or particular matter not covered by the annual report I shall be glad to look for that information.
Clause stands.
Progress reported.

speechtext:
What is the nature of the services made available by the hospital design division of the Department of National Health and Welfare?
Answer by: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
The hospital design division of the Department of National Health and Welfare provides a consulting service to all agencies interested in the design and operation of hospitals, and co-operates with the provinces
Question
in promoting sound planning of health institutions of all types.
A constant research program in the field of hospital construction is maintained by this division. The information is compiled and made available to those interested in that field when requested.
All plans submitted by hospitals on behalf of which the provinces request assistance under the national health program are reviewed by the hospital design division to ensure that such plans conform to the general standards of hospital construction as prepared by this division, and to determine the amount of federal assistance. These minimum standards have done much to ensure reasonably good accommodation for patients throughout Canada.
